author: Fowler
title: Improving Language Model Compression through Task-Specific Layer-wise Distillation
abstract: A significant challenge in layer-wise distillation is the tendency for the student model to under-fit, which stems from its reduced model capacity compared to the teacher. This problem is compounded because the teacher's hidden representations include information not essential for the student's learning of the target task. In this compression approach, knowledge is transferred by having the student imitate the hidden representations from each intermediate layer of the teacher. To mitigate these issues, we put forward a new task-aware method for layer-wise distillation. Our proposed method utilizes task-aware filters at every layer to align the student and teacher hidden representations, selectively extracting knowledge from the teacher that is pertinent to the target task. Consequently, this approach diminishes the knowledge discrepancy between the models, enabling the student to achieve a superior fit for the target task. The method's performance was evaluated under two conditions: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. Results show that our approach provides substantial and consistent advantages over established distillation techniques in both scenarios. The implementation code has been released for public access.

author: Johnson
title: A Method for Reducing Gender Bias in Language Models During Distillation by Reversing Gendered Roles
abstract: A significant issue with language models is their tendency to exhibit biases, such as incorrectly linking specific genders to professions that are not gender-specific. Without fairness constraints, the process of knowledge distillation can pass on or even intensify these biases from a teacher to a distilled model. We introduce a technique to address this by learning a fair model as part of the distillation workflow, aiming to lessen gender disparity in generated text. Our proposed method makes two alterations to the conventional distillation process, both based on swapping gender roles: one adjusts the teacher's output probabilities, and the other augments the dataset used for training. We assessed gender polarity concerning professions in text generated by the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models. Our findings indicate a considerable decrease in gender disparity, with only a small reduction in the model's overall utility. Finally, it was noted that language models with lower gender polarity in text generation do not necessarily show greater fairness in their embeddings or in their performance on downstream classification tasks.

author: Hill
title: Applying a Deep, Hierarchical Framework to Lifelong Learning in the Minecraft Environment
abstract: We introduce a system for lifelong learning intended for the Minecraft domain, an unsolved and high-dimensional problem. The proposed system is able to transfer and reuse knowledge between tasks while effectively retaining its previously acquired knowledge-base. Knowledge transfer is accomplished by learning reusable skills, which are then incorporated into a novel hierarchical deep reinforcement learning network architecture. This integration happens via two techniques: a deep skill array and a new variation of policy distillation we developed for learning skills. Our distillation method enables the architecture to retain knowledge efficiently and thus to scale for lifelong learning, as it accumulates information and condenses multiple reusable skills into one distilled network. In tests conducted on sub-domains of Minecraft, the hierarchical architecture showed superior performance and reduced learning sample complexity relative to the standard Deep Q Network.

author: Walker
title: Optimizing the Teacher in Knowledge Distillation with a Meta Learning Framework
abstract: In contrast to conventional knowledge distillation (KD) methods that employ a teacher model with fixed parameters, we introduce a simple and effective approach grounded in a meta learning framework. This technique enables the teacher network to learn to transfer knowledge more proficiently to a student network by utilizing feedback signals from the resulting student's performance. Furthermore, our method incorporates a pilot update mechanism, which serves to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and the meta-learner for meta learning algorithms that prioritize inner-learner improvement. Across various benchmarks, experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves significant improvements over traditional KD algorithms. The approach is also less sensitive to the selection of student capacity and various hyperparameters, which facilitates the deployment of KD on a wider range of models and tasks.

author: Doyle
title: A Distillation Framework for Recommender Systems Combining Latent Knowledge and Relaxed Ranking
abstract: We introduce a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender systems that enables a compact student model to learn from a cumbersome teacher model. This framework allows the student to acquire knowledge from the latent information encoded in the teacher as well as from its predictions. The first of two methods, which transfers latent knowledge directly from the teacher, uses 'experts' and a new expert selection strategy to effectively distill the teacher's extensive knowledge into the student model's limited capacity. The second method transfers knowledge from the teacher's predictions, taking into account the relaxed ranking orders between items. This approach overcomes a key limitation of state-of-the-art methods, which concentrate solely on making the student imitate the teacher's predictions and thus incompletely convey the teacher's knowledge. Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used in modern recommender systems to lower inference latency while preserving performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art competitors, achieving performance on par with or even superior to the teacher model alongside a faster inference time.

author: Rhodes
title: Knowledge Distillation for Lifelong Language Learning
abstract: A significant challenge in lifelong language learning (LLL) is avoiding the performance degradation that occurs when training on a stream of diverse tasks, as compared to multi-task versions. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a simple and efficient method that mitigates this degradation and can be readily applied to existing LLL architectures. In our approach, a teacher model is first trained on a new task as it is introduced. That teacher then transfers its knowledge to the main LLL model via knowledge distillation. The LLL model is thereby able to adapt more effectively to the new task while preserving its previously acquired knowledge. Experimental results show our proposed method yields consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art models. For both text classification and sequence generation tasks, the performance gap relative to multi-task models is substantially closed.

author: Mcclain
title: Distilling Knowledge by Aligning Internal Representations
abstract: Standard knowledge distillation trains a compact student model to reproduce the behavior of a complex teacher model. This process compresses the teacher's knowledge by optimizing the student with soft-labels derived from the teacher's output probabilities. A potential issue arises with a very large teacher, as successful transfer of its internal knowledge is not assured. The student's internal representations might be substantially different, despite a close match with the teacher's soft-labels. Such a discrepancy can hinder the transfer of the teacher's generalization abilities, a key objective of the procedure. This paper proposes a distillation approach focused on the internal representations of a large model like BERT, transferring them to a simplified student. We present two different formulations for this type of representation distillation, along with a variety of algorithms to carry it out. Experiments on datasets from the GLUE benchmark provide consistent evidence that supplementing soft-label distillation with knowledge from internal representations results in a more potent method.

author: Miller
title: Improving Accuracy on Spoken Question Answering via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A significant challenge in spoken question answering (SQA) is that machines must deeply comprehend intricate spoken material. The performance of question answering systems relies heavily on automatic speech recognition (ASR), but recent findings confirm that ASR produces very noisy transcripts, which substantially restricts a machine's comprehension abilities on the SQA task. To overcome this problem, we introduce a new distillation framework. We put forward a training method that executes knowledge distillation (KD) from both spoken documents and the corresponding written versions. Our contribution moves toward using a language model's knowledge as a supervision signal, which can result in superior student accuracy by reducing the disparity between automated and manual transcriptions. Experimental results on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset show our method’s performance exceeds that of several leading language models.

author: Henderson
title: Adversarial Learning for Multi-Model Ensemble Distillation
abstract: Ensembles of multiple base-level networks are frequently the top-performing deep neural models. The substantial storage and inference time costs associated with these ensembles, however, make them impractical for use cases involving large test sets like ImageNet. This work introduces a method to compress a complex, trained ensemble into one network by distilling knowledge from multiple trained deep neural networks (DNNs) and transferring it to a single student DNN. To facilitate the distillation of diverse knowledge from different teacher models, we employ an adversarial learning strategy. We introduce a block-wise training loss that simultaneously guides the student network to recover the knowledge from the teachers and encourages a discriminator network to differentiate between teacher features and student features. This adversarial method for transferring distilled knowledge offers three notable benefits: (1) The student network, which learns using discriminators, achieves a better optimization state than the original model. (2) A single forward pass enables fast inference, with performance that is superior to traditional ensembles of multiple source models. (3) The student can learn distilled knowledge from a teacher model with any structure. The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated by extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet datasets. On ImageNet, a student based on ResNet-50 obtains 21.79% top-1 and 5.99% top-5 validation error, an improvement of 2.06% and 1.14% over the original model.

author: Robinson
title: Training Teacher Networks to Improve Efficacy in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This paper introduces a new knowledge distillation method for enhancing the conveyance of dark knowledge from a teacher network to a student. In contrast to prevailing techniques which emphasize student model training with a given pretrained teacher, our approach focuses on learning teacher models specifically engineered to be more suitable for knowledge transfer. To achieve this, the presented algorithm concurrently optimizes student branches during the teacher model's training phase, thereby producing student-amenable representations. Because the principal contribution is a teacher-training methodology and the distillation step itself is conventional, this approach can supplement most current distillation methods to elevate the accuracy and convergence speed of various students. The proposed method yields outstanding accuracy across several well-known distillation techniques for many teacher and student model pairings, including when their architectures are dissimilar and when there is no foreknowledge of the student model during teacher training.

author: Wagner
title: A Self-Distillation Method for Natural Language Processing
abstract: Deep learning models have achieved notable success across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, in some instances performing better than humans, which can be attributed to their capacity for efficient knowledge representation. While numerous approaches exist for learning better representations, using soft target probabilities from pretrained networks for knowledge distillation has proven effective for training other models. This paper presents a new knowledge distillation method that leverages the soft target probabilities generated by the training model itself. The approach distills information with multiple modes from the word embedding space directly preceding the softmax layer. Due to computational expense, our technique approximates these soft target probabilities. To evaluate its effectiveness, the proposed method was tested on two separate and foundational NLP applications: neural machine translation and language models. The results of these experiments show that our proposed method delivers improved performance for the selected tasks.

author: Johnson
title: A Theoretical Analysis of Knowledge Distillation for Wide Neural Networks: Bounding Risk, Data Efficiency, and the Imperfect Teacher Case
abstract: A firm theoretical basis for knowledge distillation is currently missing, despite its success in model compression and knowledge transfer, a technique where a student network learns from a teacher's soft output. Recent work on the neural tangent kernel, however, allows a wide neural network to be approximated by a linear model of its random features. This paper leverages that insight for a theoretical analysis of knowledge distillation with a wide neural network. We first derive a transfer risk bound for the linearized network model. Next, we propose a metric called data inefficiency to measure a task's training difficulty. This metric shows that a high ratio of soft labels is beneficial with a perfect teacher. For an imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct the teacher's erroneous predictions, providing a rationale for the common practice of mixing soft and hard labels.

author: Gonzalez
title: Knowledge Distillation Using Collaborative Teachers for Step-by-Step Guidance
abstract: The deployment of deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices is hindered by their high storage and computational requirements. Knowledge distillation is a technique for training a compact student network through the transfer of knowledge from a larger, pre-trained teacher model. Many current distillation methods, however, neglect the useful information contained in the training process and focus only on the final results. This work introduces a novel knowledge distillation strategy that leverages two distinct teachers. The first, a teacher trained from scratch, provides the student with step-by-step assistance using its intermediate outputs. This process encourages the student network to approximate the optimal learning path toward final logits with high accuracy. A second, pre-trained expert teacher directs the student’s focus toward a critical region of features more relevant to the task. By combining the guidance from these two specialized teachers, the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation is substantially improved. Evaluations on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet datasets confirm that the proposed method for knowledge distillation is effective and achieves state-of-the-art results.

author: Santos
title: Knowledge Distillation Through Channel-Wise Attention
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to transfer a teacher network's learned knowledge to a student network, which allows the student to have fewer parameters and computations while achieving accuracy close to the teacher's. In this work, we introduce a novel distillation method composed of two transfer strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer approach is founded on channel-wise attention, which is used to convey channel information from the teacher to the student. The second approach is a guided knowledge distillation strategy. In contrast to standard Knowledge Distillation (KD), which makes the student imitate the teacher's prediction distribution for every sample, our guided method only requires the student to mimic the teacher's correct outputs. The final component is a strategy of decaying the teacher's influence. Throughout the training procedure, the weight of the distillation loss is progressively reduced. This is done to let the student gradually assume control over the optimization, rather than the teacher. The proposed method was assessed on CIFAR100 and ImageNet. On the ImageNet dataset, we reached a 27.68% top-1 error with a ResNet18 model, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieved the surprising finding that the student's performance exceeded the teacher's.

author: Gardner
title: Distillation for Adversarial Robustness
abstract: This work examines how adversarial robustness is transferred from a teacher to a student network during knowledge distillation. We find that a student can acquire substantial robustness even when distillation occurs using only clean images. To improve this process, we introduce a method for distilling robustness onto student models. Similar to conventional distillation, our approach yields small models with high test accuracy, but it also transfers the greater robustness of the large teacher network to the student. Experimental results demonstrate that student models from our method achieve decisively higher robust accuracy than adversarially trained networks that have an identical architecture, exceeding state-of-the-art results on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we show that recent techniques for fast adversarial training can be adapted to our method to achieve more rapid robust distillation.

author: Robinson
title: A Theoretical Examination of Ensembles, Knowledge Distillation, and Self-Distillation for Deep Learning Models
abstract: This work presents a formal investigation into the mechanisms by which ensembles of deep learning models improve test accuracy and how knowledge distillation can transfer this advantage to a single model. We consider a particularly difficult case where the ensemble results from averaging the outputs from several independently trained neural networks. These networks possess the same architecture, are trained with the same algorithm on the same data, and differ exclusively in the random seeds for their initialization. Our analysis indicates that ensemble and knowledge distillation methods in deep learning function very differently from concepts in traditional learning theory, like boosting or neural tangent kernels (NTKs). To properly explain them, we introduce a theory which shows that for data with a characteristic we label “multi-view”, ensembles of independently trained networks provably yield better test accuracy. Such superior accuracy can also be provably passed to a single model by training it to match the ensemble's output rather than the true labels. Our findings provide a new understanding of how ensembles work in deep learning that is completely separate from classical theorems and clarifies how “dark knowledge” is contained within ensemble outputs for use in distillation. Finally, we establish that self-distillation can be interpreted as an implicit combination of ensembling and knowledge distillation for enhancing test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Knowledge Distillation from Deep Networks for Pose Regression
abstract: We introduce a new technique for knowledge distillation from a deep network trained for pose regression, with the goal of producing an efficient Visual Odometry (VO) model. Successful knowledge transfer in typical distillation depends on "dark knowledge", which is absent in pose regression tasks. Compounding this issue, teacher predictions can be inaccurate. To address these challenges, our proposed method selectively transfers knowledge primarily in instances where the teacher model is deemed trustworthy. This is accomplished by utilizing the teacher's loss as a confidence score, which dynamically adjusts the importance assigned to the teacher's predictions. This confidence score is incorporated into the student's training in two ways: through a loss function that promotes attentive imitation for the main task, and via an attentive hint-based method for learning the teacher's intermediate features. We believe this to be the first successful application of knowledge distillation for a deep network performing pose regression. Evaluations on the KITTI and Malaga datasets demonstrate that the student's predictions closely match the teacher's. This performance is achieved while reducing parameters by as much as 92.95% and increasing computational speed by a factor of 2.12.

author: Pacheco
title: Decision Boundary-Informed Knowledge Distillation Using Adversarial Samples
abstract: A classifier's generalization ability is highly dependent on the quality of its decision boundary, implying that a well-performing classifier must have a suitable one. This suggests that for knowledge distillation, transferring information pertaining to the decision boundary could be a particularly effective strategy. To achieve this, we leverage an adversarial attack as a tool to locate samples that support the decision boundary. The proposed algorithm then uses these identified adversarial samples to train a student classifier, thereby communicating more precise information about the boundary. While many approaches to knowledge distillation have been proposed, enhancing the process remains an important research goal. Our experiments validate that this method provides a tangible improvement for knowledge distillation and reaches state-of-the-art performance.

author: Smith
title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation through the Quantification of Learned Concepts
abstract: This paper investigates why knowledge distillation is effective by testing three hypotheses. First, a deep neural network (DNN) learns more visual concepts through distillation than from raw data. Second, distillation fosters simultaneous learning of diverse visual concepts, unlike the sequential learning seen with raw data training. Third, it provides more stable optimization directions. To test these ideas, we introduce a method that quantifies and analyzes task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts found within a DNN's intermediate layers. We designed three corresponding mathematical metrics to evaluate the network's feature representations. Experimental results from diagnosing various DNNs confirmed the validity of all three hypotheses.

author: Shaffer
title: Improving Neural Machine Translation through Sample-Selective Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent research direction for boosting the performance of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems, typically involving the transfer of a teacher's knowledge for every training instance. Prior work has paid little attention to the differential effects and relationships among these instances, which serve as the conduits for transferring the teacher's knowledge. In this work, we introduce an innovative protocol for analyzing the varied influence of training samples by comparing different ways to partition them. Extensive experimentation with this protocol shows that more teacher knowledge is not necessarily better; knowledge distilled from specific samples can be detrimental to the overall distillation outcome. To address this finding, we propose two straightforward yet powerful selection strategies, operating at the batch-level and global-level, to identify suitable samples for distillation. Our approaches were evaluated on two substantial machine translation tasks: WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results confirm that our methods achieve gains reaching +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points, respectively, when compared to the Transformer baseline.

author: Wolfe
title: Utilizing Generative Replay for Robust and Memory-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A significant challenge in Data-Free Knowledge Distillation is the student model's experience of knowledge degradation, caused by a distribution shift in the synthetic data used for training. For a data-free method to be practical, it should produce a student with monotonically improving accuracy. However, typical approaches rely on a validation set to identify the point of peak performance, and such a set may not be available. A simple solution to the distribution shift problem involves storing and replaying generated samples, but this incurs substantial memory costs and introduces privacy risks. We propose an alternative that models the distribution of past synthetic samples using a generative network. Our approach uses a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a customized training objective to optimally learn representations of the synthetic data. Through a generative pseudo replay process using samples from the VAE, the student is rehearsed, thereby preventing knowledge degradation without any sample storage. On image classification benchmarks, experiments show our method optimizes the expected distilled model accuracy while simultaneously eliminating the memory overhead of sample-storing techniques.

author: Peterson
title: An Analysis of Knowledge Distillation for Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) models offer major speed improvements compared to autoregressive models because they predict entire output sequences in parallel. To achieve better performance, existing NAT models frequently use knowledge distillation, where training data is generated by a pre-trained autoregressive system. Although knowledge distillation empirically provides large accuracy gains for NAT, the reasons for this success have remained unclear. In this work, we carry out systematic experiments to discover why knowledge distillation is so vital to the training of NAT models. We establish that the technique helps NAT models to account for variations in output data and also serves to reduce dataset complexity. Additionally, a strong link is noted between an NAT model's capacity and the ideal complexity of the distilled data for obtaining the best possible translation quality. Informed by these discoveries, we put forward several new approaches for altering dataset complexity to enhance NAT model performance. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results among NAT-based models and reduce the performance difference relative to the autoregressive baseline on the WMT14 En-De benchmark.

author: Moore
title: An Attention-Based Approach to Feature Matching in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to transfer generalized information from a pre-trained teacher model to a student network to guide its training. A prevalent strategy involves manually selecting and connecting intermediate features of the teacher and student to facilitate this transfer. This manual selection process, however, frequently establishes links that are not optimal, thereby constraining the performance gains from distillation. A prior method has sought to resolve this issue, but identifying highly effective links under practical conditions remains difficult. We present a feature distillation technique that is both effective and efficient, leveraging all teacher feature levels without requiring manual link specification. Our approach uses an attention-based meta-network to learn the relative similarities between features. These identified similarities are then used to moderate the distillation strength for every potential teacher-student feature pair. As a consequence, our method finds potent links more efficiently than the previous work and demonstrates improved performance on model compression and transfer learning benchmarks. We also provide further qualitative analyses and ablation studies to clarify how our method facilitates superior distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Employing Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Teacher Selection in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The deployment of pre-trained deep models in production for natural language processing (NLP) applications is significantly hampered by slow inference speeds and large GPU memory requirements. Knowledge distillation serves as a popular model compression technique, enabling a small student model to acquire knowledge from one or more large teacher models. For distillation involving multiple teachers, current state-of-the-art approaches typically employ a fixed weight for each teacher throughout the entire training process. It is also common for existing techniques to assign an equal weight to all teachers. This paper observes that student models can achieve better performance by learning from teachers differentially, a consequence of varying training example complexity and the student model's own capabilities. We have systematically formulated a reinforcement-based method to dynamically assign weights to different teacher models for each training instance, with the objective of optimizing student model performance. The feasibility and effectiveness of our method are clearly demonstrated through extensive experimental results across several NLP tasks.

author: Rogers
title: Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers Using a Confidence-Based Approach
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation, which originally used supervision from one teacher for student training, has been extended by recent methods that use multiple teachers to improve student performance. A key issue with existing approaches is their tendency to merge knowledge by averaging teacher predictions or using other label-free schemes. This can mislead the student if some teacher predictions are low-quality. To address this problem, we introduce a method that assigns an adaptive, sample-specific reliability weight to each teacher's prediction by utilizing ground-truth labels. Under this scheme, predictions that are closer to one-hot labels receive larger weights. The proposed method also incorporates features from intermediate layers to create a more stable knowledge transfer process. Through extensive experiments, our approach is shown to consistently achieve better results than all compared state-of-the-art methods across a range of teacher and student architectures.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial Online Knowledge Distillation Guided by Feature Maps
abstract: While feature maps hold valuable information regarding spatial correlation and image intensity, prior online knowledge distillation methods have focused exclusively on class probabilities. In this work, we present an online knowledge distillation technique that leverages an adversarial training framework to transfer knowledge from both feature maps and class probabilities. The method involves training multiple networks at the same time, where discriminators learn to differentiate the feature map distributions among them. Each network is paired with a discriminator that is trained to label its own network's feature map as fake and the other's as real. A network is then trained to deceive the associated discriminator, thereby encouraging it to learn the feature map distribution of the other network. We show our proposed method surpasses conventional direct alignment methods like L1 and is more appropriate for online distillation. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks simultaneously. When applied to classification tasks using different network architectures, our technique yielded a substantial performance increase, especially when a small network was trained in a pair with a large one.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Deep Graph Neural Network Compression
abstract: While deep graph neural networks (GNNs) demonstrate high expressiveness for modeling graph-structured data, their over-stacked architectures create difficulties for deployment and rapid testing on mobile or embedded systems. Knowledge distillation, using a teacher-student architecture, is an effective technique for compressing such GNNs. The central step in this process is quantifying the discrepancy between the teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. A major drawback, however, is that a uniform distance metric may be ill-suited for graphs of varying structures, and determining the optimal distance formulation is a challenging problem. We introduce a novel adversarial knowledge distillation framework for graph models to address these issues. This framework adaptively detects and reduces the discrepancy by adversarially training a discriminator and a generator. The success of deep GNNs is largely due to their effective capture of inter-node and inter-class correlations. Accordingly, our method proposes to evaluate the inherited knowledge from both node-level and class-level perspectives using a trainable discriminator. This discriminator is trained to distinguish teacher knowledge from what the student has learned, while the student GNN, acting as a generator, attempts to fool the discriminator. We believe this work is the first to apply adversarial training to knowledge distillation within graph domains. Experiments conducted on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks show that the proposed method boosts student performance by a significant margin. The outcomes imply that our framework can accurately transmit knowledge from a complex teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

author: Munoz
title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks Without Access to Training Data
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to have a smaller model (the Student) learn from a high-capacity source model (the Teacher) to approximate its high level of performance. Existing methods for training the Student rely on the original training data or on meta-data extracted from that data. However, gaining access to the dataset that the Teacher was trained on is not always practical, either because the dataset is extremely large or due to privacy and safety considerations, as with bio-metric or medical data. In this paper, we therefore introduce a novel, data-free approach to train the Student from the Teacher. Our method synthesizes data impressions from the complex Teacher model, using these impressions as stand-ins for the original training data samples to transfer learning to the Student via knowledge distillation, all without the use of any meta-data. We call this approach a data-free method and show on multiple benchmark datasets that our framework produces competitive generalization performance comparable to what is attained by distillation using the actual training data.

author: Roman
title: Achieving Fairness for Visual Recognition Through Feature Distillation
abstract: Fairness represents a progressively critical challenge for computer vision, most notably for systems that make decisions concerning humans. A model that yields indiscriminative outcomes for protected groups exhibits algorithmic fairness, but achieving this remains an open problem. In this work, we present a systematic method for reducing algorithmic biases in visual recognition tasks via feature distillation. While distillation techniques have been broadly used to increase prediction accuracy, to our knowledge, no previous work has explicitly focused on also improving fairness with distillation. We also offer a theoretical justification for our proposed method concerning its impact on knowledge distillation and fairness. Extensive experiments show that our approach substantially mitigates bias against certain minorities, which we demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world face datasets without any sacrifice of accuracy.

author: Blair
title: A Systematic Examination of Policy Distillation Approaches
abstract: In practice, many different formulations for policy distillation exist. Although the technique is conceptually simple and widely used, subtle differences between these formulations can significantly impact the optimization objective and the resulting performance. This work presents a thorough exploration across the landscape of policy distillation, assessing the rationales and advantages of each variant through both empirical and theoretical analysis. A key tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning is the transfer of knowledge between policies, which has been successfully applied to enhance agent optimization, resulting in stronger performance achieved faster on more difficult domains. Our results identify three distillation techniques as preferable, with the best selection being contingent on task-specific characteristics. A newly introduced distillation method that incorporates expected entropy regularization, in particular, permits faster learning across a wide array of situations while still ensuring convergence.

author: Herrera
title: Knowledge Distillation for Object Detectors Through Granular Feature Imitation
abstract: The computational demands of leading CNN-based recognition models often make them unsuitable for deployment on devices with limited resources. Knowledge distillation is a promising technique to overcome this obstacle by training a small student model to mimic the output of a large teacher model, which improves its ability to generalize. However, existing distillation approaches have largely concentrated on the simpler problem of classification, neglecting more complex tasks like object detection. We establish that applying standard knowledge distillation to a detection model provides only a small benefit. To meet the specific challenges of distilling knowledge for detectors, we introduce a method based on the imitation of fine-grained features, which capitalizes on the spatial variation in feature responses. Our central idea is that detectors place a higher emphasis on local areas surrounding objects. Therefore, the differences in feature responses at anchor locations near objects encode important information about the teacher model's generalization behavior. We have engineered a new mechanism to identify these specific locations and compel the student model to imitate the teacher's features there, resulting in improved performance. We first test this approach on a lightweight detector developed to represent the basic ideas of modern anchor-based models. On the demanding KITTI dataset, our method yields an increase of up to 15% in mAP for the student model over its counterpart trained without imitation. We then conduct extensive evaluations using the Faster R-CNN model on the Pascal VOC and COCO benchmarks in several scenarios. The proposed imitation technique reduces the performance gap between the student and teacher models by as much as 74%.

author: Dudley
title: Improving Single-Model Reading Comprehension via Knowledge Distillation with Answer Alignment
abstract: This work addresses two key limitations of modern machine reading comprehension systems: their reliance on large, computationally expensive ensembles and their fragility when faced with adversarial examples. We utilize knowledge distillation to transfer the predictive capabilities of a complex teacher ensemble into a compact, single student model. The investigation begins by confirming that a standard knowledge distillation setup for answer span prediction is a viable strategy for this task. We then introduce two novel distillation methods designed to enhance this process. These methods incorporate guidance from the ensemble's alignment information and introduce a penalty for predictions on confusing, incorrect answers. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach. Our best student model is 12 times faster during inference than the teacher ensemble, with only a marginal 0.4% drop in F1 score on the SQuAD test set. Moreover, the student model achieves superior performance compared to the teacher on the NarrativeQA benchmark as well as on adversarial SQuAD datasets.

author: Gray
title: Compressing BERT through a Strategy of Progressive Module Replacement
abstract: We present a new approach for BERT compression based on the progressive replacement of modules. In contrast to knowledge distillation methods, our technique does not require any additional loss function. The process involves first dividing the original BERT model into multiple modules and then creating compact substitutes for each one. We train the compact modules by stochastically swapping them with the original modules, which encourages them to imitate the originals' behavior. The probability of this replacement is gradually increased throughout the training period. This method fosters a deeper level of interaction between the compact and original models. On the GLUE benchmark, the proposed approach achieves better performance than existing knowledge distillation techniques, opening up a new perspective on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: A Re-evaluation of How Knowledge Distillation Functions
abstract: Knowledge distillation is a common technique where a compact student network is trained to replicate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble. Although this method can improve student generalization, we demonstrate it does not usually operate as is widely supposed. A large disparity often persists between the predictive distributions of the teacher and student, even when the student has enough capacity to perfectly emulate the teacher. We establish that optimization challenges are a primary cause for the student's failure to match the teacher. We also reveal that the dataset used for distillation affects the fidelity of the student's imitation, and that a closer match paradoxically fails to consistently produce better student generalization.

author: Calderon
title: Improving Model Generalization for Vehicle Routing Problems Using Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning models for vehicle routing problems often fail to generalize across different data distributions because they are typically trained and evaluated on instances from a single, uniform distribution. To address this generalization gap, we introduce a knowledge distillation framework designed to produce deep models with enhanced performance on novel data. The approach employs multiple teacher models, each specialized on a distinct exemplar distribution, to transfer knowledge to a single student model. This results in a student that is both compact and capable across various distributions. A key component is an adaptive mechanism that directs the student's learning toward more challenging distributions, allowing for more efficient acquisition of difficult-to-learn knowledge. Comprehensive experimental evidence shows that, when evaluated against standard neural approaches, our method obtains competitive performance on unseen data from both in-distribution and out-of-distribution sources. These test cases include instances that were synthetically generated and those from established benchmarks like TSPLIB and CVRPLIB. Furthermore, the proposed technique is broadly applicable and notable for its lower computational requirements during inference.

author: Montgomery
title: A Dynamic Graph Framework for 3D Object Detection
abstract: We introduce an architecture for 3D object detection from point clouds, motivated by recent 2D models that operate without non-maximum suppression. In contrast to typical pipelines that rely on intricate workflows and dataset-specific domain expertise, our approach formulates detection as message passing on a dynamic graph. This method generalizes the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects, a construction that eliminates any need for post-processing such as object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. We also propose a set-to-set distillation strategy customized for 3D detection to facilitate learning from sparse point clouds. This strategy aligns teacher and student model outputs in a permutation-invariant manner, which greatly simplifies knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. On autonomous driving benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. A thorough analysis of the detection model and distillation framework is also presented.

author: Hensley
title: Enhancing Low-Precision Network Performance with Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning networks that achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on computer vision tasks like object detection and image classification are typically large models with many parameters. A major difficulty with these top-performing models after training is their deployment on resource-constrained inference systems, as such networks are often intensive in their compute and memory needs. The use of low-precision numerics and model compression through knowledge distillation are two common techniques for lowering the computational requirements and memory footprint for these models. In this paper, we explore the synthesis of these two methods, showing that knowledge distillation techniques can be used to significantly improve the performance of low-precision networks. Using our approach, state-of-the-art accuracies are reached on the ImageNet dataset with ResNet architecture variants at ternary precision and 4-bit precision. We introduce three schemes that allow for the application of knowledge distillation techniques at different phases of the train-and-deploy workflow.

author: Ray
title: Using Knowledge Distillation to Convey Inductive Biases
abstract: For many tasks, possessing appropriate inductive biases is critical, particularly when computational resources or data are limited, or when the training data fails to perfectly represent test-time conditions. The process of defining, engineering, and efficiently adjusting these inductive biases, however, is not always simple. In this work, we examine the potential of knowledge distillation to transfer the impact of inductive biases from one model to another. We employ families of models that possess different inductive biases, such as LSTMs versus Transformers and CNNs versus MLPs, placing them in tasks and situations where the correct inductive biases are paramount. Our study analyzes the impact of inductive biases on the solutions to which models converge and probes how, and to what degree, knowledge distillation transfers this impact, evaluating not just performance but also other characteristics of the final solutions.

author: Bush
title: Enhancing Multi-Label Image Classification Using Knowledge Distillation from a Weakly-Supervised Detection Model
abstract: We present a novel and efficient deep framework for improving multi-label image classification. The proposed method utilizes knowledge distillation, transferring information from a weakly-supervised detection task that requires no bounding box annotations. The process begins by developing a weakly-supervised detection model using only image-level data. This model then serves as a teacher to a multi-label classification student model within an end-to-end framework. Guidance is provided through a knowledge distillation module, which leverages the teacher's class-level predictions for the entire image and its object-level visual features for object RoIs. While other approaches also use region-level cues, they typically depend on laborious object-level annotations, a requirement our method avoids. Through this cross-task knowledge distillation, the classification model's performance is significantly enhanced. Moreover, efficiency is maintained as the teacher model can be discarded during inference. Comprehensive evaluations on two large-scale datasets, MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE, show that our framework achieves superior results relative to state-of-the-art methods on measures of both performance and efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Relational Distillation for Link Prediction without Graph-based Inference
abstract: For predicting links, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) exhibit strong performance. However, their practical deployment is limited by high latency stemming from a dependence on neighborhood data. Conversely, Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are efficient but substantially less effective because they lack relational knowledge. To combine the strengths of these models, we first investigated direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods, such as matching either predicted logits or node representations. Observing that these direct KD approaches are not effective for this task, we introduce a relational KD framework for transferring knowledge to an MLP student. In contrast to simple KD techniques that match independent outputs, the proposed method distills relational information focused around individual anchor nodes. We employ two complementary strategies: a rank-based matching approach and a distribution-based one. Extensive experimentation shows that this framework significantly improves the performance of MLPs on link prediction. The student model even surpasses its teacher GNN on seven out of eight benchmarks and provides a 70.68x inference speedup compared to the GNN for link prediction on the OGB large-scale dataset.

author: Perez
title: Domain Adaptation Using One or More Black-Box Source Predictors
abstract: This paper addresses a practical and significant unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) setting where adaptation in the target domain proceeds using only black-box source models, for which just network predictions are accessible. For this problem, a novel two-step knowledge adaptation framework is presented. The first stage distills knowledge from the source predictor into a custom target model, accounting for the structure of the target data. The second stage involves fine-tuning the distilled model to better conform to the target domain. This framework does not mandate that neural networks have identical architectures across domains, which permits effective adaptation on devices with low resources. UDA seeks to transfer knowledge from previously labeled source datasets to a new unlabeled target, alleviating the need for labeling. However, preceding methods usually require raw source data to perform data-dependent alignment in a transductive fashion, which can raise privacy issues for the source individuals. Even some recent studies using white-box models may inadvertently leak raw data through generative adversarial learning. Our empirical results from three UDA scenarios (single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) establish that the proposed method obtains highly competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art data-dependent techniques. The implementation code has been made available.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Deep Neural Network Interpretability by Means of Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The considerable complexity of Deep Neural Networks makes reasoning about their predictions challenging. This opacity hinders their deployment in practical situations that require interpretability, such as mission-critical or ethically-sensitive applications, despite their widespread success in fields from speech recognition and computer vision to language modeling. To overcome this problem, we utilize the Knowledge Distillation technique. Our approach distills a Deep Neural Network into a decision tree with the goal of simultaneously attaining interpretability and high performance. We frame the task as a multi-output regression problem. Experiments show that for a given tree depth, the student model's accuracy is significantly higher than that of a vanilla decision tree, with performance gains of approximately 1% to 5%. To ensure scalability for big datasets, the experiments were carried out using the TensorFlow platform. To our knowledge, this work is the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees for multi-class datasets.

author: Miller
title: An Investigation of BERT-Based Rankers Under Distillation
abstract: The high computational demands during inference for deep language models like BERT hinder their use in real-world search scenarios. This paper examines if and how the search-related knowledge inside BERT can be transferred to a more compact ranker via distillation. Knowledge contained within these large models enables them to identify intricate matching signals between queries and passages, providing a major performance improvement for state-of-the-art information retrieval systems. Our experimental findings highlight the critical importance of using a proper distillation process, which can achieve a speedup of up to nine times while maintaining top-level performance.

author: Hall
title: Accommodating Heterogeneous On-Device Models in Resource-Constrained Federated Learning via Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer
abstract: A common limitation of existing federated learning algorithms is the requirement for uniform on-device models, a constraint that excludes devices with limited computational resources. To accommodate the diverse nature of modern devices, we introduce a novel framework that supports heterogeneous on-device models by employing a Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer mechanism. Our approach gives individual devices the autonomy to select model architectures that align with their available local resources. Knowledge is transferred among these disparate models using a specially designed zero-shot distillation technique. In contrast to previous work relying on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator, our method has no such prerequisites. Furthermore, the computationally demanding distillation task is handled by the central server, thereby enabling resource-limited devices to participate. On the server, an adversarial process trains a generator against an ensemble of the received on-device models. The resulting central knowledge is then communicated back to each client as parameters tailored to its specific model, facilitating simple integration. Comprehensive experiments validate the proposed framework's robustness and effectiveness under various difficult federated learning conditions, including model and data heterogeneity, the presence of stragglers, and server agnosticism to on-device knowledge.

author: Garcia
title: Size Reduction of Visual-Linguistic Models Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations has advanced considerably, research into small VL models remains limited. This paper investigates knowledge distillation (KD) as a means to compress a large transformer-based VL model into a more compact student model. The central difficulty stems from the differing object detectors used by the teacher and student, which generate inconsistent regional visual tokens and consequently misalign their hidden representations and attention distributions. To surmount this challenge, we adapt the teacher model by retraining it with region proposals from the student's detector, while using features from the teacher's original detector. Once the network inputs are aligned, the adapted teacher can successfully transfer knowledge from its intermediate representations. Specifically, the method utilizes a mean square error loss to match the attention distribution inside each transformer block and a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align hidden states by differentiating them from a queue of negative samples. We demonstrate that our distillation approach substantially boosts the performance of small VL models on visual question answering and image captioning. The distilled model obtains a 120.8 CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an increase of 5.1 over the version without distillation, and achieves 69.8 accuracy on VQA 2.0, a gain of 0.8 over the baseline. Comprehensive experiments and ablations validate the effectiveness of this VL distillation strategy during both the pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

author: Ramirez
title: Self-Knowledge Distillation Using Progressively Refined Targets
abstract: A wide array of regularization strategies, including restricting the function space, introducing randomness into the training process, and data augmentation, has led to substantial gains in the generalization performance of deep neural networks. In this paper, we put forward a simple and effective regularization technique wherein a model progressively distills its own knowledge to soften hard targets (such as one-hot vectors) over the course of training. This approach can be understood within the knowledge distillation framework, with a model serving as its own teacher. To be specific, targets are adaptively modified by blending the ground-truth with the model's own prior predictions. We show that the proposed method creates an effect similar to hard example mining by rescaling gradients as a function of classification difficulty. The technique is applicable to any supervised learning problem with hard targets and combines readily with existing regularization methods to yield further improvements in generalization. It is also confirmed that our method not only delivers superior accuracy but also produces high-quality confidence estimates with respect to both calibration and ordinal ranking. Comprehensive experimental results across three different domains—image classification, object detection, and machine translation—demonstrate that our approach consistently improves upon state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Distilling Models with Low-Cost Convolutions
abstract: To address the challenge of deploying neural networks in memory-limited settings, we introduce a method for structural model distillation. The student architecture is a direct structural transformation from the teacher, which avoids any redesign and permits the use of identical hyperparameters. Using attention transfer for the distillation of residual networks, we characterize the trade-off between memory and accuracy across four benchmark datasets with Pareto curves and tables. Our results show that substantial reductions in memory are attainable for a very small accuracy penalty. We also confirm that the performance of a student network created through distillation exceeds what is achieved by training that same student architecture directly from data. This work contributes to the nascent field of flexible memory reduction, where the associated cost-benefit is not yet well established.

author: Diaz
title: Utilizing a Two-Stage, Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation for the Compression of Web Question Answering Systems
abstract: For model compression in web Question Answering systems, we introduce a two-stage method that uses knowledge distillation from multiple teachers. In the first stage, a student model is pre-trained on a general Q&A distillation task. For the second stage, this student is fine-tuned on downstream tasks, such as Web Q&A and the GLUE tasks MNLI, SNLI, and RTE, with multi-teacher distillation. This strategy reduces the overfitting bias from individual teacher models and helps transfer more general knowledge. The motivation for this work is that while models like BERT and OpenAI GPT excel at question answering, their large parameter counts result in slow inference, hindering practical deployment. Conventional compression methods typically cause information loss, leading to reduced performance. Our experiments show the proposed method significantly surpasses baselines, delivering a substantial speedup in model inference while obtaining results that are comparable to the original teacher models.

author: Wood
title: A Statistical Viewpoint on Effective Data Augmentation within Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The interaction between data augmentation (DA) and knowledge distillation (KD), a training technique where a student model is guided by a teacher model, has been insufficiently explored. While KD research has focused on the network output side, for instance by designing better loss functions, the input side has been largely unexamined. This work investigates why certain DA methods, such as CutMix, consistently deliver superior performance in KD and what constitutes a beneficial DA strategy in this setting. From a statistical perspective, our analysis indicates that an effective DA scheme should lower the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. We propose a practical, empirically justified metric for this purpose: the standard deviation of the teacher's mean probability. In addition to this theoretical understanding, we introduce a new data-mixing DA approach that is based on entropy and designed to improve upon CutMix. Our claims are supported by extensive empirical studies, which demonstrate that selecting a better DA scheme is a simple way to achieve considerable performance gains in knowledge distillation.

author: Clark
title: A Distillation Method for Universal Style Transfer at Ultra-High Resolutions
abstract: The use of universal style transfer is often restricted by the substantial model size of the deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, such as VGG-19, which supply rich representations but create memory bottlenecks for ultra-resolution images. This work puts forward a new knowledge distillation technique for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer that diminishes the number of convolutional filters. The central concept relies on an observation that a unique collaborative relationship is formed by encoder-decoder pairs, a relationship we define as a novel kind of knowledge for these models. Furthermore, a linear embedding loss is utilized to address the mismatch in feature sizes that occurs during distillation, guiding the student network to acquire a linear embedding of the features from the teacher. Broad experimentation validates our method's efficacy with various universal style transfer techniques (WCT and AdaIN), maintaining performance even after the model is compressed by 15.5 times. In particular, we achieve for the first time universal style transfer on images over 40 megapixels on a 12GB GPU by applying our method to compressed WCT models. The generality of our algorithm is confirmed by additional experiments on optimization-based stylization approaches, showing its effectiveness across different stylization paradigms. Our source code and pre-trained models are publicly accessible.

author: Adams
title: An Investigation of Distillation, Warmup, and Learning Rate Restart Heuristics
abstract: This work utilizes mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), two recent methods for representation and loss surface analysis, to examine several deep learning heuristics. We apply these techniques to knowledge distillation and the learning rate strategies of (cosine) restarts and warmup, with the objective of hypothesizing the mechanisms behind their success. Such an approach contrasts with prior empirical analyses that rely on tools like linear interpolation and visualizations based on dimensionality reduction, which have notable limitations. Controlled experiments are valuable because heuristics like normalization layers, skip connections, knowledge distillation, and learning rate schedules have yielded significant improvements in the convergence speed and final performance of widely used models, yet their theoretical foundations are not well understood. Our investigation provides empirical evidence suggesting that: (c) during distillation, latent knowledge from the teacher is primarily conveyed to the deeper layers of the student; (b) learning rate warmup appears to prevent training instability originating from the deeper layers; and (a) the explanations frequently given for the success of cosine annealing are not supported by our findings.

author: Zuniga
title: An Online Distillation Approach to Large-Scale Distributed Neural Network Training
abstract: While ensembling and distillation methods can enhance model quality, their use in industrial contexts is often impeded by increased test-time costs and complex training pipelines, respectively. This work investigates an online distillation technique that is substantially easier to deploy, since it circumvents elaborate multi-stage setups and adds a minimal number of new hyperparameters. We first assert that this method permits the use of extra parallelism to train on very large datasets with a speedup of roughly twofold. This acceleration is notably possible even beyond the point where additional parallelism ceases to benefit either synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. The mechanism involves two neural networks, trained on disjoint data partitions, that share information by compelling each model to align with the predictions of its peer. These peer predictions can be generated from a stale copy of the other model's weights, which allows for infrequent communication. We secondly assert that online distillation offers an economical method for dramatically improving the reproducibility of a model's exact predictions. To substantiate these claims, we present results from experiments conducted on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest neural language modeling dataset constructed to date, containing 6x10^11 tokens from the Common Crawl repository.

author: Wong
title: A Regularized Knowledge Distillation Approach for Domain Generalization
abstract: A significant challenge hindering the practical use of convolutional neural networks is their limited ability to generalize when faced with data that is not sufficiently representative. In this work, we introduce a training strategy that is simple, effective, and can be easily integrated into existing pipelines. This proposed method is based on a knowledge distillation framework and incorporates a novel gradient filter as a regularization term. We determined that the generalization capacity of the model is enhanced because the learning of the mapping is made easier, an effect we attribute to the gradient filter and the "richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network. Our framework's ability to substantially improve generalization for deep neural networks is demonstrated through extensive experiments. In a comparison with current state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques, our method shows superior results across different tasks like image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning. To conclude, we put forward two new metrics for analyzing our approach, allowing for a clearer understanding of how it benefits the generalization of deep neural networks.

author: Lynch
title: A Re-evaluation of Knowledge Distillation through Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: The effectiveness of Knowledge Distillation (KD) is not solely attributable to the inter-category similarity information provided by teachers; the regularization from soft targets is an equally or perhaps more critical component. This perspective challenges the conventional practice of only using strong teacher models to guide weaker students. We support this claim with two empirical findings: first, that a student model can markedly improve its teacher when the distillation process is reversed, and second, that a student can still be significantly enhanced by a poorly-trained teacher with substantially lower accuracy. These observations are explained by our theoretical analysis, which establishes a connection between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that KD constitutes a form of learned label smoothing regularization and that label smoothing regularization can function as a virtual teacher model for KD. Based on this understanding, we introduce a novel distillation framework that operates without a teacher. In this method, the student model learns either from its own outputs or a manually specified regularization distribution. The approach yields performance comparable to standard KD with a superior teacher, making it valuable when no strong teacher is available. This generic method can be used directly for training deep neural networks. Without incurring additional computational expense, it provides up to a 0.65% performance gain on ImageNet relative to established baselines and outperforms label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Mutual Contrastive Learning for Teacher-Free Online Knowledge Distillation in Visual Recognition
abstract: In teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD), an ensemble of student models undergoes collaborative training, distilling knowledge from one another. While current online KD methods perform well, they usually concentrate on class probabilities as the principal knowledge type, thereby neglecting useful information from feature representations. We introduce a framework for online KD that is grounded in mutual contrastive learning. The fundamental principle of our method is to facilitate the mutual transfer of contrastive distributions among a group of networks in an online fashion. This approach aggregates embedding information from across the networks and maximizes the lower bound of the mutual information between network pairs. Consequently, each network learns supplementary contrastive knowledge from the others, which yields superior feature representations and boosts performance on visual recognition tasks. We extend our method beyond the final layer to intermediate layers, using an adaptive layer-matching scheme trained with meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning for visual recognition show that our layer-wise method achieves consistent performance improvements over state-of-the-art online KD approaches. This outperformance demonstrates that the proposed layer-wise technique guides networks to generate higher-quality feature representations.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation Independent of Training Data
abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has advanced significantly as a method for model compression and transferring knowledge, its application is limited by the fact that most existing techniques are data-driven. These algorithms typically presuppose access to large quantities of original or alternative training data, which is frequently unavailable in practical settings. To overcome this challenging limitation, we introduce a novel adversarial distillation mechanism for training a compact student model in the complete absence of real-world data. We formulate an optimizable upper bound for a new metric, termed model discrepancy, which quantitatively measures the difference between the teacher and student models. In our framework, a generator adversarially creates difficult samples intended to maximize this discrepancy, while the student and teacher models function jointly as a discriminator to minimize it. Extensive experiments reveal that the performance of our data-free method is comparable to that of established data-driven approaches. Impressively, our technique can be applied without modification to the more complicated domain of semantic segmentation, where it achieves state-of-the-art results. The source code and pretrained models can be found online.

author: Martin
title: Improving Sequence-to-Sequence ASR Models via Knowledge Distillation from BERT
abstract: To supply sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) ASR models with both left and right context, we employ knowledge distillation from BERT, which serves as an external language model. This overcomes a limitation of attention-based seq2seq models, whose left-to-right decoding process restricts them to left context only. In our method, the training of the seq2seq ASR is guided by soft labels generated from BERT. We also investigate using context that extends beyond the current utterance as an input for BERT. Evaluations on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) show our method achieves a significant improvement in ASR performance relative to the seq2seq baseline. Using BERT for knowledge distillation is superior to using a transformer LM that is restricted to left context. We also demonstrate the benefit of leveraging context beyond a single utterance. The proposed method performs better than other ways of applying LMs, such as shallow fusion and n-best rescoring, and adds no extra cost during inference.

author: Gray
title: Enhancing Feature Distillation Through the Use of a Projector Ensemble
abstract: This work examines the role of the feature projector connecting student and teacher models, an element that has remained largely unstudied in feature distillation. Prior research has instead concentrated on designing loss functions and choosing which layers to distill. We put forward a plausible mechanism for the projector's function, supported by empirical results. Our investigation begins with the finding that a student network gains an advantage from a projector, even when its feature dimensions already match the teacher's. We frame the direct training of a student backbone as a multi-task learning scenario, where the model must concurrently extract discriminative features for its classification objective and align its features with the teacher's for distillation. It is our hypothesis, confirmed experimentally, that lacking a projector leads the student to excessively conform to the teacher's feature distributions, regardless of its distinct architecture and weight initialization. This overfitting degrades the quality of the deep features the student uses for classification. By contrast, adding a projector disentangles these two learning goals. This allows the student network to better focus on its primary feature extraction duty while still being guided by teacher features via the projector. Motivated by this positive function, our work introduces a method based on a projector ensemble to further improve student feature quality. The efficacy of this approach is validated by experimental outcomes on multiple datasets across a range of teacher-student pairings.

author: Mayo
title: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Analysis of Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This work investigates the bias-variance tradeoff associated with using soft labels for knowledge distillation. Although recent findings indicate that soft labels act as a regularizer, a role typically linked to variance reduction, their precise effects on bias and variance have not been well understood. Knowledge distillation is a process where a student network learns under the supervision of soft labels provided by a teacher model's outputs. Our analysis reveals that the tradeoff between bias and variance is not constant but varies on a per-sample basis during training. We identified a specific set of samples, termed regularization samples, that cause an increase in bias alongside a decrease in variance. At a constant distillation temperature, we observed that a greater quantity of these regularization samples negatively correlates with distillation performance. Nevertheless, we also found empirically that performance deteriorates if these regularization samples are completely excluded. These findings prompted the development of a novel method using weighted soft labels, which is designed to help the network adaptively balance the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. The effectiveness of our proposed method is validated through experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks.

author: Bowman
title: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Representations of Speech
abstract: The quality of speech representations has greatly improved with self-supervision, but the on-device deployment of leading embedding models is often impeded by their significant resource requirements and lack of public availability. To address these limitations, our work offers a publicly released set of paralinguistic speech models that are compact while delivering performance near the state-of-the-art. Our technique is grounded in knowledge distillation, with models trained exclusively on public data. We examined various architectures, carrying out a thorough evaluation of our models using the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. At less than 15% of the original model's size (314MB vs 2.2GB), our largest distilled model was trained on 6.5% of the data and reaches over 96% of the accuracy on six out of seven tasks. The most compact model has a size of 22MB (1%) and attains over 90% of the accuracy on six of seven tasks. Our models demonstrate superior performance to the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on six of seven tasks. Moreover, our smallest model surpasses the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks, while being only 7% of its size.

author: Hawkins
title: An Efficient Knowledge Distillation Method for Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a valuable technique for visual tasks like supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning. However, its standard application is inefficient, as the significant computational expense is dominated by forward passes through large teacher networks. A recent method, ReLabel, addresses this by pre-computing a single label map for an entire image, from which region-level labels are extracted for cropped views using RoI align, thus avoiding numerous passes through the teacher. A notable drawback of this technique is a reduction in performance caused by inconsistencies between the global label map and the local region labels, a problem that arises because the teacher models are trained using a multi-crop methodology. We introduce a new, fast knowledge distillation framework that generates soft labels by emulating the multi-crop KD training procedure. Our approach trains more rapidly than ReLabel because it omits post-processing operations such as RoI align and softmax. In scenarios involving multi-crop data loading from the same image, our method is even more efficient than a conventional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, a ResNet-50 model trained with our method reaches 79.8% accuracy, which is about 1.0% higher than ReLabel and achieved with greater speed. The efficiency gains of our framework are also confirmed on a self-supervised learning task.

author: Cohen
title: An Attention-Based Combinatorial Approach to Intermediate Layer Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation serves as a method for training and compression, coupling a teacher and a student neural network during the training process. The student network attempts to replicate the outputs of the teacher, which is presumed to be a highly accurate predictor. A student with a less complex architecture is generally chosen to enable model compression while preserving high performance. In many cases, distillation is confined to the final predictions, though the student could also gain from the teacher's guidance on its internal components. This motivated our investigation into distillation for intermediate layers. Because a direct one-to-one mapping between the layers of the student and teacher may not exist, current methods often skip some teacher layers, using only a subset for distillation. We propose a combinatorial technique using attention to address this deficiency, which negatively affects quality. Our approach synthesizes information from the teacher by weighting the importance of each layer.
