Distillation is then performed between the combined representation of the teacher layers and the layers of the student. We applied our technique to distill a 12-layer BERT model into smaller 6-, 4-, and 2-layer students, which we evaluated on tasks from the GLUE benchmark. The results from our experiments indicate that our combinatorial method can achieve superior performance compared to other existing approaches.

author: Cameron
title: The Crucial Role of Pre-training for the Performance of Compact Models
abstract: The high cost of utilizing large, pre-trained models for downstream applications, a common paradigm in modern natural language representation, has motivated research into model compression. These large models are typically trained on vast general-domain text with self-supervision. However, we show that an overlooked baseline of simply pre-training and then fine-tuning a compact model can perform competitively against more intricate methods from concurrent work, establishing that pre-training is also vital for smaller architectures. Building on this, we explore a simple, general, and effective algorithm that yields further improvements. This method first pre-trains a compact model and then uses standard knowledge distillation to transfer task-specific knowledge from a large, fine-tuned model. Our extensive experiments more broadly probe the interaction between pre-training and distillation with respect to two under-studied variables: model size and the properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising discovery is that these two steps have a compounding effect, even when executed sequentially on the same data. To stimulate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models available to the public.

author: Parsons
title: A Curriculum Learning Strategy for Distillation in Dense Retrieval
abstract: The distillation of ranking knowledge from a base re-ranking model is a demonstrated method for creating more effective dense retrieval models. We introduce a general optimization framework that utilizes curriculum learning to regulate the difficulty of the training data generated by a teacher re-ranking model. Our approach progressively optimizes the student dense retrieval model by supplying it with knowledge distillation data of increasing complexity. To be specific, the student model is first trained with coarse-grained preference pairs derived from the teacher's ranking, after which the process transitions to using more fine-grained pairwise requirements for document ordering. In our experimental evaluation, we employed a straightforward implementation of this framework to augment two current state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Evaluations conducted on three public datasets for passage retrieval show the utility of our proposed method.

author: Perez
title: Improving Multi-Task Natural Language Understanding Networks via Distillation from Single-Task Models
abstract: Training multi-task neural networks to a level where they can match or outperform their single-task equivalents presents a significant challenge. To overcome this, we leverage knowledge distillation, using single-task models as teachers for a multi-task student model. We augment this training with a novel annealing procedure that provides a gradual transition from the distillation loss to a supervised learning objective, which assists the multi-task model in exceeding the performance of its teachers. Our methodology is assessed on the GLUE benchmark through multi-task fine-tuning of BERT. The proposed method yields consistent gains when compared against conventional single-task and multi-task training.

author: Stewart
title: Using Knowledge Distillation for Private Compression of Deep Learning Models
abstract: The growing popularity of intelligent mobile applications creates a need to deploy powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on user devices. However, the superior performance of DNNs is often tied to highly complex models, resulting in computational requirements that overwhelm the capacity of mobile hardware. A further complication arises because training these sophisticated DNN models depends on large volumes of user data, which can contain sensitive information. The direct deployment of such models introduces a prohibitive privacy risk for users. To address these capacity and privacy obstacles for on-device deep learning, we have designed a framework for private model compression. Operating within the knowledge distillation paradigm, our method employs a joint strategy of hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. To enforce differential privacy, the knowledge transferred from the cumbersome teacher model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed with noise. We also introduce an elegant technique for selecting query samples, which reduces the total number of queries and thus controls the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations, including an implementation on an Android mobile device, confirms that the proposed method both compresses large models efficiently and furnishes a strong privacy guarantee. On the SVHN dataset, for example, a compact model from our method attains a 20x compression ratio and a 19x speed-up with an accuracy loss of only 0.97%, while satisfying a meaningful differential privacy guarantee of $(9.83,10^{-6})$.

author: Adams
title: An Empirical Investigation of the Supposed Incompatibility Between Knowledge Distillation and Label Smoothing
abstract: This work conducts an empirical examination of the recent perspective that knowledge distillation is incompatible with label smoothing. The basis for this claimed conflict is that relative information among teacher logits is lost during label smoothing. We establish a novel connection illustrating how label smoothing influences the distributions of classes that are semantically close versus those that are distant. A new metric is also introduced to quantitatively assess the amount of information erased from a sample's representation. Through extensive analyses, visualizations, and comprehensive experiments covering Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation, we argue that this incompatibility view is both one-sided and imperfect. Finally, we provide a broad discussion of several situations where the utility of label smoothing is indeed compromised.

author: Clark
title: Model-Agnostic Federated Learning Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We investigate the feasibility of a universal federated learning interface that allows an arbitrary group of agents to collaborate. Such an interface must be model-agnostic, making no presuppositions regarding the agents' model architectures, and must function without any representative public data. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most evident technique for developing such protocols. Surprisingly, however, we find that most straightforward federated learning protocols based on KD exhibit poor performance. To understand this, we introduce a new theoretical framework using kernel ridge regression in a federated setting, which can account for both data and model heterogeneity. Our analysis reveals that this performance decline is mainly attributable to a core limitation of knowledge distillation when faced with heterogeneous data. We validate our framework by using it to analyze and develop new KD-based protocols. Experiments on real-world tasks using neural networks confirm that the performance of these protocols, although not yet satisfactory, is accurately predicted by our theoretical model.

author: Hahn
title: A General Distillation Approach for Object Detectors Using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: Training compact object detectors often employs knowledge distillation (KD), though this technique remains under-explored for heterogeneous detectors. Our empirical work reveals that a student can benefit from superior FPN features from a dissimilar teacher, despite differences in their detection heads and label assignment methods. However, two issues arise when distillation is attempted through direct alignment of feature maps. First, overly strict constraints can be imposed on the student due to discrepancies in feature magnitude separating the teacher and student. Second, the gradient of the distillation loss can be dominated by FPN stages and channels from the teacher possessing large feature magnitudes; this can overwhelm the impact of other features during KD and introduce substantial noise. To counter these problems, we propose a method that uses the Pearson Correlation Coefficient to imitate features, thereby focusing on relational information from the teacher while relaxing constraints on feature magnitude. The proposed technique consistently shows better performance than existing detection KD methods and is effective for both homogeneous and heterogeneous pairings of students and teachers. It also converges faster. When a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin model acts as the teacher, a RetinaNet model with a ResNet-50 backbone attains 41.5% mAP and an FCOS model reaches 43.9% mAP on the COCO2017 benchmark. These results are 4.1% and 4.8% greater than their baselines, respectively.

author: Walter
title: Enhanced Knowledge Distillation Using a State-of-the-Art Teacher
abstract: This work introduces a new method for knowledge distillation that is designed for scenarios involving a very strong teacher, unlike most existing approaches which are evaluated in settings with less competitive teacher models. We empirically observe that when a teacher is significantly more capable, the divergence between its predictions and a student's can become quite large. As a consequence, forcing an exact match of predictions via KL divergence can interfere with training and cause conventional methods to perform badly. We show that preserving the relational structure between teacher and student predictions is sufficient. A correlation-based loss is proposed to explicitly capture the intrinsic inter-class relationships from the teacher. Recognizing that instances vary in their semantic similarity to each class, we also extend this relational matching to the intra-class level. The presented technique is straightforward and effective. Extensive experimentation confirms that it adapts well to different architectures, model scales, and training procedures, consistently achieving state-of-the-art results on tasks in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

author: Edwards
title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning via Knowledge Distillation from a Cross-Domain Ensemble
abstract: In Federated Learning (FL), a central model is trained collaboratively by local nodes that never share their training data. Conventional FL methods, which often use parameter sharing or co-distillation to manage unbalanced data distributions, introduce communication overhead and significant privacy risks. This paper presents a communication-efficient and privacy-preserving FL approach based on one-shot offline knowledge distillation. The method uses unlabeled public data from an external domain to transfer knowledge. For enhanced privacy protection without compromising accuracy, we propose creating a quantized and noisy ensemble of predictions from the fully trained local models. Extensive evaluations on image and text classification tasks demonstrate that our privacy-preserving method surpasses baseline FL algorithms in both communication efficiency and accuracy.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Models through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We present a method that utilizes knowledge distillation to synthesize the advantages of probabilistic topic models with those of pretrained transformers. This modular approach integrates easily with any neural topic model, serving to enhance topic quality. We validate its utility on two models with dissimilar architectures, achieving state-of-the-art levels of topic coherence. The flexible framework improves results not only for aggregate performance across all topics, a frequently used measure, but also yields benefits when directly comparing corresponding topics. Topic models are widely applied to extract human-interpretable themes from extensive collections of documents.

author: Foster
title: Predicting Click-Through Rates with Ensemble-Based Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning models are now widely applied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction, yielding higher accuracy in numerous industrial contexts. However, the majority of current research is dedicated to engineering intricate network architectures for modeling complex feature interactions and dynamic user activities. Such increased model complexity can result in slower online inference, creating an obstacle for adoption in real-time systems. In contrast, our study introduces a new model training methodology founded on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning paradigm for passing knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. This strategy not only enables the simplification of the student into a vanilla DNN model but also produces major accuracy gains relative to state-of-the-art teacher models. These advantages motivated our further exploration into using a powerful teacher ensemble for more accurate training of the student model. We also put forward several novel techniques that facilitate CTR prediction with ensembles, including teacher gating and early stopping guided by distillation loss. Thorough experiments were performed against 12 existing models using three industrial datasets. The efficacy of our training strategy using KD is supported by the results of both offline and online A/B testing.

author: Rocha
title: A Method for Network Compression with Limited Data Using Layer-wise Distillation
abstract: Obtaining light-weighted deep neural networks via model compression is a widely used strategy. However, leading methods typically depend on fine-tuning with large amounts of training data to preserve accuracy, which can be at odds with privacy and security requirements. This paper examines the problem of network compression in a few-shot context: how a network can be compressed effectively with only a minor loss in performance, given just a few examples per class. The central challenge for few-shot network compression is the high estimation error from the original model during inference, as the smaller network is prone to overfitting the small training set. Such estimation errors can propagate and compound through each layer, which ultimately degrades the network's output. To counteract this problem, we introduce a novel knowledge distillation technique that operates layer-wise. By interleaving the hidden layers of the teacher and student models, the layer-by-layer accumulation of estimation errors is substantially reduced. This proposed method constitutes a general framework that is compatible with common network compression approaches like pruning. Thorough experiments using benchmark datasets establish that our method can considerably boost the student network’s accuracy when only a few training examples are provided.

author: Ellis
title: A Study of Distilling Representations for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates whether preserving the global topology of a teacher's data embeddings can serve as a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, given that real-world graphs frequently contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We introduce an approach based on contrastive learning that implicitly maintains global structure by aligning the student and teacher node embeddings in a shared representation space. This differs from prior GNN distillation techniques, like the Local Structure Preserving loss, which focus on matching local relationships over edges between the embeddings. Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for enhancing resource-efficient GNNs with guidance from more expressive, cumbersome teacher models. We also present an expanded suite of benchmarks using large-scale, real-world datasets where a significant performance disparity exists between the teacher and student models. Experiments on 4 datasets using 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs. Our approach surpasses the local structure preserving baseline, a global structure variant of that baseline, and methods adapted from 2D computer vision. A concluding analysis of representational similarity shows our method achieves a balance in preserving local and global relationships, unlike structure-preserving approaches which tend to excel at one over the other. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns.

author: Baker
title: Enhanced Utilization of Parallel Data for Low-Frequency Words in Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models are frequently trained using synthetic data produced through knowledge distillation (KD). For low-frequency words, however, a disparity exists between the distilled and the original data, which increases the prediction error rate for these words. We mitigate this problem by directly using the raw data in the NAT training regimen via a pretraining stage. Our analysis of directed alignments indicated that while KD creates more deterministic alignments from low-frequency source words to targets, it fails to generate a sufficient number of alignments from low-frequency target words to the source. Based on this finding, we propose a reverse knowledge distillation procedure to create more alignments for infrequent target words. We combine these complementary techniques into a unified training strategy to maximize the benefit from both authentic and synthetic data, thereby improving NAT performance. Experiments were performed on five translation benchmarks with two advanced architectures. The results indicate that the proposed method provides significant and generalizable enhancements to translation quality by lowering the number of errors on low-frequency words. The method achieves BLEU scores of 28.2 on the WMT14 English-German dataset and 33.9 on the WMT16 Romanian-English dataset.

author: Wright
title: Using Distilled Semantics for Holistic Video Scene Analysis
abstract: We present a framework that learns depth, motion, and semantics jointly from monocular video to advance holistic scene understanding. Our approach employs a novel training protocol combining knowledge distillation with self-supervision, alongside a compact network architecture for efficiency on both GPUs and embedded platforms. While depth and motion are learned without explicit ground truth, supervision for semantics is provided by distilling proxy ground truth from a pre-trained teacher network. This work builds upon recent findings that geometry and motion can be learned from video alone, bypassing the difficult task of sourcing ground truth annotations for them. A thorough evaluation shows our method obtains state-of-the-art outcomes for monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and the task of motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Utilizing Knowledge Distillation in a Federated Setting
abstract: In many distributed learning frameworks, model parameters are exchanged between workers as a substitute for sharing raw data. Federated learning, for example, shares the gradients or weights of each neural network model. For modern deep neural networks with a very large number of parameters, this approach becomes exceedingly costly, especially under constrained communication resources. Federated distillation (FD) presents a compelling solution for distributed learning by exchanging only model outputs, whose dimensions are frequently much smaller than the models' parameter counts (for instance, the 10 labels of the MNIST dataset). The purpose of this chapter is to furnish a deep understanding of FD, showcasing its communication efficiency and its broad applicability to various tasks. To achieve this and demystify FD's operational principles, the first section of this chapter offers a novel asymptotic analysis for knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), two of FD's foundational algorithms, by leveraging neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. The second section subsequently describes a baseline FD implementation for a classification problem and demonstrates its accuracy and communication efficiency performance against FL. To conclude, the third section highlights the suitability of FD for diverse distributed learning tasks and contexts by presenting two specific applications: its use over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and its application to reinforcement learning.

author: Baker
title: Fusing Diverse Classifiers into a Single Model Using Distillation
abstract: This work addresses the challenge of consolidating the knowledge from an ensemble of classifiers into one model. The constituent classifiers possess varying architectures and are trained on distinct sets of target classes, and the only data available for this consolidation process is a general collection of unlabelled examples. Such a challenge arises in situations involving multiple data sources that are prohibited from sharing their raw data, for instance due to privacy restrictions, permitting only the exchange of pre-trained models. Furthermore, limitations on data access at each source can prevent any single one from covering all classes, while discrepancies in available computing power may lead to the use of different model architectures. We introduce a method for merging these heterogeneous classifiers that extends the principles of knowledge distillation. Our approach is founded on a derived probabilistic connection between the outputs from the source classifiers and the overall probability distribution across the union of all classes. From this connection, we develop two distinct families of techniques, one employing cross-entropy minimization and the other matrix factorization. These techniques enable the estimation of soft labels spanning the complete class set from unlabelled data, which then serve as training targets for the final unified classifier, substituting for true labels. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on the ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our methods. The proposed techniques yield substantial performance gains over a baseline approach that naively adapts distillation. Moreover, the resulting unified classifier reaches an accuracy level nearly equivalent to that of a model trained conventionally with centralized access to all supervised data.

author: Richards
title: A Generative Adversarial Network Approach to Text Generation Using Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have produced outstanding results in high-quality image generation for computer vision, their application to NLP is impeded by the discrete character of text. We introduce an approach that effectively adapts the GAN setup for text generation by incorporating knowledge distillation. In our method, autoencoders (AEs) are utilized to generate a continuous representation for sentences. This smooth representation, which assigns non-zero probabilities to more than one word, is then distilled, training the generator to synthesize analogous smooth representations. Such work is relevant for many important NLP applications, including machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. We validated our idea with multiple experiments across different datasets. The proposed technique demonstrates superior performance over conventional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training, evaluated using the BLEU score and the Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure.

author: Hurst
title: A Distillation Framework for Compact and High-Performing Ranking Models in Recommender Systems
abstract: This work introduces a new method for training ranking models for applications like recommender systems to be both compact and highly performant. Our approach adapts knowledge distillation, a technique that has demonstrated success in achieving efficiency and effectiveness in image recognition, to the specific domain of learning to rank. The core idea involves using a large, pre-existing teacher model to provide supervisory signals that guide the training of a smaller student model, in addition to learning from the training data. This process results in a student model with a substantially smaller size for more efficient online inference, while retaining a ranking performance level comparable to that of the much larger teacher model. A key advantage of this framework is its modularity, as it is independent of the specific architectures chosen for the student and teacher models; we also resolve particular difficulties associated with applying distillation to ranking. Validation on public benchmarks with state-of-the-art models for recommendation confirms that our method meets its objectives. Specifically, the student model produced by our method is less than half the size of the teacher, yet it obtains a similar ranking quality and significantly outperforms an identical student model trained without distillation.

author: Ross
title: Distilling Knowledge from Ensembles for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: The performance of a student network can be improved by training it to learn from a more powerful teacher network, a method known as knowledge distillation. Because sentence translation with a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is a time-intensive task, using a smaller model is desirable to accelerate this process. We show how the translation quality from an ensemble teacher and an oracle BLEU teacher network can be transferred into a single NMT system. We also report translation gains from a teacher that has an identical architecture and dimensionality to the student network. Training the student model remains computationally demanding, so we propose a data filtering method that uses the teacher model's knowledge. This approach not only expedites training but also improves final translation quality. Our methods are applicable to any NMT architecture without code modifications to speed up decoding.

author: Robinson
title: Improving Non-Autoregressive Translation by Correcting Teacher-Induced Lexical Choice Errors
abstract: This study empirically identifies an unintended consequence of training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models with knowledge distillation (KD): the student model inherits lexical choice errors for low-frequency words from its autoregressive teacher. While KD is critical for simplifying raw data, this propagation of errors is a notable side effect. To mitigate this issue, we propose a method that exposes the NAT model to the original raw data, thereby restoring valuable information about infrequent words lost during distillation. Our technique incorporates an additional Kullback-Leibler divergence term, which is calculated from the difference between the NAT model's word selection and the one present in the raw data. The broad effectiveness and universality of our method are demonstrated by experiments across multiple model architectures and language pairs. Our claim that performance gains are driven by a reduction in lexical choice errors on low-frequency words is substantiated by extensive analyses. Encouragingly, our technique sets a new state-of-the-art for NAT, achieving 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. The source code will be made available.

author: Bright
title: Efficient and Distilled Models for Practical Lipreading Applications
abstract: A substantial gap remains between existing lipreading techniques and the requirements for real-world application, despite advances in the field driven by neural networks focused on architecture and generalization. Our work introduces a set of innovations designed to close this gap. We propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel head built with Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Networks, which dramatically cuts the computational cost relative to an already efficient baseline. By applying self-distillation, we also elevate state-of-the-art accuracy by a wide margin, reaching 88.5% on LRW and 46.6% on LRW-1000. We further demonstrate that knowledge distillation is a highly effective mechanism for transferring this high performance to the proposed lightweight models. This process results in a family of models with a range of accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. The most promising of these compact models achieve performance on par with the previous state-of-the-art, yet with an 8.2-fold reduction in computational cost and a 3.9-fold reduction in parameter count. We believe these contributions will help enable the deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios.

author: Hicks
title: Adapting Models to New Domains via Instruction from Teacher Models
abstract: Domain adaptation is essential for real-world scenarios where training and test data distributions differ. A major limitation of previous Deep Learning approaches is the requirement for joint training on both source and target domain data, which is undesirable when adapting to many domains or to a domain that is evolving, like spam detection with its shifting adversarial tactics. To address this problem, we present an approach that extends Knowledge Distillation to the domain adaptation setting. For unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources, we demonstrate how a student model can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark. The model accomplishes this by incorporating the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers along with the similarities between their domains. When only a single teacher is available, using domain similarity to assess its trustworthiness is not effective. For this situation, we put forward a simple metric that shows a strong correlation with the teacher's accuracy on the target domain. We establish that by integrating high-confidence examples chosen via this metric, the student model can obtain state-of-the-art results in the single-source case.

author: Williams
title: Data-Free Knowledge Transfer by Adversarially Matching Teacher Predictions
abstract: Distilling information from a large teacher network into a smaller student model is a common objective in contemporary deep learning. However, this task is frequently complicated by a lack of access to the teacher's original training data, often due to the enormous size of datasets or increasing privacy constraints. We introduce a new technique that trains a student to replicate its teacher's predictions without using any data or metadata. Our method achieves this by training an adversarial generator to discover images where the student and teacher outputs diverge, and then using those images to train the student. On simple datasets such as SVHN, the student that results from our method provides a close approximation of its teacher. For CIFAR10, our technique improves upon the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (using 100 images per class), despite operating without any data. Lastly, we also introduce a metric to measure the correspondence of beliefs between a teacher and student near decision boundaries, finding a substantially higher match for our zero-shot student with the teacher than for a student distilled using real data.

author: Rodriguez
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Improving Upon Graph Neural Network Teachers
abstract: A significant challenge in machine learning is semi-supervised learning on graphs. In this domain, classification methods that rely on graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated superior performance compared to classic techniques such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated nature of these neural architectures results in a complex prediction process that may not fully exploit valuable prior knowledge contained in the data, for example, the tendency for structurally connected nodes to have the same classification. This work introduces a framework using knowledge distillation to resolve these shortcomings. Our method extracts knowledge from a trained GNN, which acts as a teacher model, and transfers it to a purposefully designed student model. The student model is composed of two elementary prediction mechanisms, feature transformation and label propagation, which are designed to naturally retain feature-based and structure-based prior knowledge. We specifically implement the student as a trainable combination of parameterized modules for feature transformation and label propagation. The trained student is therefore able to leverage both this prior knowledge and the distilled knowledge from the GNN teacher to generate more effective predictions. Moreover, the prediction process of the trained student model is more interpretable than that of GNNs. We performed experiments on five public benchmarks, utilizing seven different GNN architectures as teacher models: GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP. The results of our experiments indicate that the learned student consistently surpasses its corresponding teacher model, with performance gains averaging between 1.4% and 4.7%.

author: Burton
title: Efficient Large-Scale Language Representations via Hardware-Friendly Block Structured Pruning of Transformers
abstract: Large-scale pre-trained language models are characterized by their high accuracy across numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the widespread deployment of these models is constrained by hardware limitations in weight storage and computational speed, a challenge that is particularly acute for edge computing. This paper introduces a method for creating efficient, large-scale language representations from transformers by utilizing hardware-friendly block structure pruning. For optimization, our technique incorporates the reweighted group Lasso within the block-structured pruning framework. The proposed approach yields high compression rates, resulting in a significant decrease in both weight storage and computation. Experimental evaluations on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark with models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT indicate that our method can provide up to 5.0x compression on some tasks with no or negligible degradation in accuracy. Moreover, our method is orthogonal to existing compact models like DistilBERT that employ knowledge distillation; we can achieve an additional 1.79x average compression rate when applied to DistilBERT with zero or minimal impact on accuracy. The final compressed model is appropriate for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Imparting Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT to Simple Neural Networks via Distillation
abstract: The field of natural language processing has seen neural networks grow progressively more deep and intricate. Deep language representation models like BERT, ELMo, and GPT exemplify this trend, leading to a belief that earlier, shallower neural architectures for language understanding are no longer useful. In this work, however, we show that it is possible to make rudimentary, lightweight neural networks competitive without any architectural modifications, additional training data, or extra input features. Our proposed method involves distilling knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a student model consisting of a single-layer BiLSTM. A siamese version of this student is used for sentence-pair tasks. We evaluate our approach on multiple datasets spanning paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, finding that it achieves performance comparable to ELMo while requiring about 100 times fewer parameters and reducing inference time by a factor of 15.

author: Henderson
title: Distilling Knowledge from Graph Neural Networks into Multi-Layer Perceptrons
abstract: For the task of node classification, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve strong results. Their practical deployment in industry is limited, however, by scalability issues that stem from data dependency. The inference process for a GNN relies on fetching neighboring nodes up to several hops away, which imposes a burden on latency-sensitive systems. While existing acceleration techniques like pruning and quantization can lower the number of Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, their effectiveness is constrained because they do not resolve the underlying data dependency problem. In contrast, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) exhibit much faster inference speeds due to their lack of graph dependency, but they generally offer lower accuracy than GNNs for node classification. These opposing characteristics motivate our approach of combining GNNs and MLPs using knowledge distillation (KD). Our research demonstrates that the performance of an MLP can be substantially boosted by using KD from a GNN. The resulting distilled MLPs, which lack any graph dependency at inference, achieve competitive accuracy while performing inference 146X-273X faster than GNNs and 14X-27X faster than other acceleration methods. In a production scenario across 7 datasets with both transductive and inductive predictions, the accuracy of the proposed method surpasses that of standalone MLPs by an average of 12.36% and matches GNN performance on 6 of the 7 datasets. A detailed analysis clarifies the conditions under which the distilled MLPs can attain accuracy comparable to GNNs, suggesting our method is a practical choice for applications with strict latency constraints.

author: Brown
title: An Integrated Framework for Compressing Vision Transformers
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have recently emerged as a popular model class. Without requiring specialized image operators like convolutions, ViTs can achieve competitive performance when trained on a massive scale. A significant drawback, however, is their prohibitive computational expense, which arises from stacked multi-head self-attention modules among other components. While extensive research and notable successes exist for compressing convolutional neural networks, the compression of Vision Transformers is a nascent field where existing methods have typically addressed only one or two compression aspects. This work presents a comprehensive framework for ViT compression that combines three effective strategies: layer skipping, pruning, and knowledge distillation. We cast the problem as an end-to-end, budget-constrained optimization that simultaneously learns model weights, layer-specific pruning ratios or masks, and configurations for skipping, all guided by a distillation loss. This optimization problem is solved using the primal-dual algorithm. We conducted experiments on the ImageNet dataset with several ViT models, including DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones, demonstrating that our method consistently surpasses recent competitors. For instance, the DeiT-Tiny model can be reduced to 50% of its original FLOPs with almost no degradation in accuracy.

author: James
title: A Self-Distillation Framework for Learning Robust Cross-Modal Representations
abstract: The CLIP learning objective is inefficient with respect to computation and data because it does not adequately handle the noisy, many-to-many correspondences in image-caption datasets harvested from the web. We introduce a new training methodology to address this problem, based on cross-modal contrastive learning. Our framework learns robust representations with greater efficiency from noisy data by using soft image-text alignments and a self-distillation procedure. For a selection of images and captions in every minibatch, the model distills its own knowledge to dynamically create soft-alignment targets, which are then used for parameter updates. Comprehensive evaluations across 14 benchmark datasets show that our method consistently surpasses its CLIP equivalent in zero-shot classification, linear probe transfer, and image-text retrieval, all without additional computational expense. An analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed indicates that our approach provides superior effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both CLIP and standard ImageNet-trained models. Finally, pretraining on datasets whose sizes span two orders of magnitude suggests that our method's advantage over CLIP scales with the quantity of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Improving Supernet Training via Alpha-Divergence
abstract: The automatic design of efficient neural architectures can be effectively achieved using weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS). This technique involves a supernet that contains all candidate architectures as its sub-networks, which are then trained in a joint process. For weight-sharing NAS to succeed, knowledge must be effectively distilled from the teacher supernet to its student sub-networks. We have found that the conventional distillation metric, KL divergence, can cause student models to incorrectly estimate the teacher's uncertainty, either by over- or under-estimating it. This issue leads to diminished sub-network performance. To resolve this, our work introduces an improved supernet training method based on a more generalized alpha-divergence. An adaptive selection of the alpha-divergence allows our approach to simultaneously avoid both over- and under-estimation of the teacher's uncertainty. We demonstrate substantial improvements by applying this training methodology to slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS. Specifically, the family of models we discovered exceeds the performance of prior art such as BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS over a wide range of FLOPs. An 80.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet is attained by our method using just 444M FLOPs. The source code and pretrained models are provided at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Improving Fake Media Detection Generalization with a Distillation-Based Continual Representation Method
abstract: The proliferation of fake media, including deepfakes and synthetic facial imagery, presents a challenge for modern multimedia technologies. While many detection techniques report high accuracy, their performance often degrades because they are trained on static datasets within constrained evaluation contexts, a common limitation in AI. To address this poor generalization, this work leverages the principles of continual learning for neural network training, with a focus on improving data efficiency. We introduce a method that integrates techniques from Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). The approach is engineered to perform sequential domain adaptation on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets. Within a teacher-student model architecture, our method is designed to effectively minimize catastrophic forgetting. Comprehensive experimental validation demonstrates that our technique is efficient at domain adaptation for detecting low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images across several datasets, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods.

author: Maddox
title: A BERT Compression Technique Using Earth Mover's Distance for Many-to-Many Layer Mapping
abstract: While pre-trained language models like BERT have demonstrated remarkable success across a range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, their substantial storage and computational demands create obstacles for deployment on resource-constrained devices. This work introduces a new distillation method for BERT founded on a many-to-many layer mapping scheme. This scheme permits every intermediate layer of the student to draw knowledge from any of the teacher's intermediate layers, enabling our model to learn adaptively from different teacher layers for various NLP tasks. To facilitate this, we utilize Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to calculate the minimum total cost of transferring knowledge from the teacher network to the student network. EMD enables an effective match for the many-to-many layer mapping. Additionally, we introduce a cost attention mechanism designed to automatically learn the layer weights used in the EMD calculation, which is expected to improve model performance and accelerate convergence. Extensive experiments conducted on the GLUE benchmark show that our model obtains competitive results compared to powerful alternatives regarding both model compression and accuracy.

author: Valencia
title: A Review of Compression Methods for Deep Learning Text Models
abstract: Over the last several years, natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have seen significant progress driven by deep learning models. Examples include Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs), along with Transformer-based architectures such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2), Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN), Extra-Long Network (XLNet), Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5), T-NLG, and GShard. A primary issue with these models, however, is their exceptionally large size. This contrasts with the needs of real-world applications, which often demand a small model footprint, low latency, and minimal power consumption. This review covers six different families of methods for model compression that enable deployment for industrial NLP tasks: Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and approaches using Sub-quadratic Transformers. Given the high demand for applications built on efficient and compact models and the vast amount of recent work on the topic, this survey aims to organize the extensive research from the 'deep learning for NLP' community of the past few years into a coherent presentation.

author: Smith
title: An Automated Search Framework for the Compression of Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Recently, more attention has been directed toward compressing Generative Adversarial Networks, driven by the increasing need to deploy GANs on mobile devices for uses such as image editing, translation, and enhancement. In contrast to the considerable efforts devoted to compressing other deep models, the field of GAN compression, which usually targets the generators, is still in its early development. Existing algorithms for GAN compression are typically restricted to particular model architectures and loss functions. Inspired by recent successes of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce an automated framework for compressing GANs. Our method operates within a custom-designed, efficient search space to conduct an end-to-end discovery of novel, efficient generators that meet specified computational budgets. Compression is achieved by guiding the search process via knowledge distillation from the original GAN model. The proposed approach is fully automatic, standalone in that it does not need trained discriminators, and generally applicable to a variety of GAN models. We assess our framework on two representative GAN applications: image translation and super resolution. Without requiring elaborate additions, this method yields exceptionally lightweight and more competitive compressed models that considerably outperform current alternatives. The source code and our pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Enhancing Activity of Daily Living Recognition through Distilled Video-Pose Embeddings
abstract: Numerous methods exist for recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) by combining RGB video with 3D poses. Differentiating these activities is challenging because they can look very similar, requiring the modeling of fine-grained details. The rigidity of modern 3D ConvNets in capturing subtle visual patterns has made approaches that fuse RGB and 3D Poses a dominant research direction. A significant drawback, however, is the high computational cost of extracting 3D poses from RGB streams without appropriate sensors, which limits the use of such methods in low-latency, real-world applications. This raises the question of how 3D Poses can be most advantageously used for ADL recognition. To answer this, we present an extension of the Video-Pose Network (VPN), a pose-driven attention mechanism, by exploring two separate strategies. The first strategy transfers Pose knowledge into the RGB modality using feature-level distillation. The second strategy mimics pose-driven attention via attention-level distillation. We then integrate both approaches into a unified model. Our proposed method is shown to be not only effective but also significantly faster and highly resilient to noise in Poses. The model surpasses representative baselines on four public datasets, achieving this superior performance with or without the availability of 3D Poses. The code has been made publicly available.

author: Maldonado
title: Knowledge Distillation Through Feature Mimicry
abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely used technique for training an efficient 'student' network by leveraging a high-capacity 'teacher' network. Conventional distillation supervises the student using the soft logits from the teacher. This work puts forth the argument that having the student imitate the teacher's features from the penultimate layer is a more effective strategy. The student can learn more useful information directly from the teacher's features, and this imitation process can be used even for teachers that lack a softmax layer. According to experimental results, this method obtains superior accuracy compared to traditional knowledge distillation. To improve feature imitation, a feature vector is separated into its direction and magnitude. We contend that the teacher should permit greater freedom for the magnitude of the student's features, allowing the student to concentrate more on mimicking the feature direction. A loss term founded on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) is proposed to accomplish this. With this new loss, our method does indeed imitate feature directions with greater precision, relaxes the constraints on feature magnitudes, and obtains state-of-the-art accuracy for distillation. A theoretical analysis is provided explaining how LSH aids in feature direction mimicry, and the application of feature imitation is extended to multi-label recognition and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: A Knowledge Distillation Method for Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are utilized for many machine learning applications, including super resolution, domain transfer, and generating synthetic data. The tens of millions of parameters in state-of-the-art GANs make them expensive to deploy on hardware with low SWAP (size, weight, and power), like mobile devices, and in applications that demand real-time operation. A survey of existing literature revealed no methods for reducing the number of parameters in GANs. We therefore present a technique for compressing GANs that relies on knowledge distillation, where a smaller "student" GAN is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger "teacher" GAN. On the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets, we show that our distillation approach can compress teacher GANs by ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, with no loss in the quality of the generated imagery. Our experiments also point to a qualitative boundary for the compression of GANs. Furthermore, we found that with a fixed budget of parameters, compressed GANs perform better than GANs trained with standard techniques. We hypothesize that the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, which enables effective training with alternating gradient descent, is a partial cause. A high-quality generative model with few parameters can thus be produced by first training an over-parameterized GAN and then applying the proposed compression scheme.

author: Davidson
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework Using Multiple Views for Robust Re-Identification
abstract: We present a training methodology using a teacher-student framework to transfer knowledge from multiple views of a target. A teacher network, exposed to a diverse set of visual perspectives, provides a supervisory signal to a student network processing fewer views. This strategy overcomes the significant performance degradation common in standard re-identification systems when moving from Video-To-Video scenarios to Image-To-Video settings. Our approach builds upon recent work transferring temporal information from video-based to image-based networks. Notably, the student model exceeds its teacher's performance and sets a new state-of-the-art for Image-To-Video re-identification by a substantial margin. We show improvements of 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. The properties of the proposed method are explored through a detailed quantitative and qualitative analysis covering Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID. The implementation for this work can be found at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: A Method for Publishing Graph Neural Networks with Guarantees of Differential Privacy
abstract: Growing concerns about the privacy of trained graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged due to their increasing use in sensitive domains such as healthcare and medicine. Specifically, even when only black-box access to a trained model is available, GNNs remain susceptible to privacy breaches like membership inference attacks. We propose a framework for preserving privacy during the release of GNN models within a centralized environment. Given access to an unlabeled public graph, our approach provides a method to release GNN models that are trained directly on public data but incorporate knowledge from private data in a manner that protects privacy. The proposed method integrates the knowledge-distillation framework with two distinct noise mechanisms, noisy labeling and random subsampling, to deliver rigorous privacy guarantees. We provide a theoretical analysis of our technique using the Renyi differential privacy framework. Additionally, we demonstrate the strong empirical performance of our method in comparison with multiple baseline approaches adapted to handle graph-structured data.

author: Graham
title: A Regularization Method for Federated Learning Using Multi-Level Auxiliary Branches
abstract: Data heterogeneity and imbalance among clients present a major obstacle in federated learning, resulting in inconsistencies across local networks and unstable global model convergence. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce a novel regularization approach based on model architecture. This method constructs several auxiliary branches within each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at multiple distinct levels. Through online knowledge distillation, the main pathway of the local model learns representations that are congruent with those from these hybrid auxiliary pathways. The proposed technique is shown to enhance the robustness of the global model, particularly in non-iid settings. It can be conveniently integrated into various federated learning frameworks without introducing additional communication costs. We present comprehensive empirical studies that demonstrate notable performance improvements in both accuracy and efficiency relative to existing methods.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks in the Absence of a Training Set
abstract: While modern model compression procedures can shrink large neural networks to a much smaller size, often with no loss in accuracy, they universally require the original training set. This requirement is a significant barrier when the dataset is extremely large or cannot be released due to privacy and safety issues, for example in biometrics tasks. We introduce a technique for knowledge distillation that functions without access to data. This method can compress deep neural networks from large-scale datasets down to a small portion of their initial size, using only supplemental metadata released with a pretrained model. The paper also examines different varieties of metadata compatible with our approach and analyzes the tradeoffs that come with using each one.

author: Mckay
title: Efficiently Compressing Large-scale Language Models Through an Augmentation-based Distillation Framework
abstract: The remarkable empirical success of large-scale language models is accompanied by substantial drawbacks, including larger models, higher power requirements, and reduced inference speed, all of which obstruct their use on low-resource hardware. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a potent framework for compressing these models. However, large neural networks often memorize their training data, resulting in predictions that lack consistency when data distributions are slightly perturbed. Furthermore, with limited task-specific data, a student model has fewer chances to extract valuable information from its teacher. To overcome these difficulties, we put forward a data-agnostic distillation framework. This method uses mixup, a simple yet powerful data augmentation strategy, to equip the final model with enhanced generalization capabilities. Specifically, the student is tasked with emulating the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of sample pairs in addition to the original training instances. We present a theoretical argument showing that, under plausible assumptions, our approach leads to a reduced gap between the generalization and empirical errors. We validate its effectiveness with experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where our method delivers consistently significant improvements over standard KD and surpasses several strong baseline methods. The advantages of the proposed framework are further supported by experiments in a limited-data context and by ablation studies.

author: Liu
title: Equipping CLIP for Multimodal Generation through Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Dual-stream architectures such as CLIP have shown success on various multimodal alignment tasks, a result of large-scale vision-language pre-training with vast amounts of image-text data. These models are nonetheless ill-suited for multimodal generative tasks due to their limited text encoders. To resolve this issue, our proposed method augments a dual-stream VLP model by integrating a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) using vision-language knowledge distillation, thereby enabling multimodal generation. This distillation technique is significantly more data- and computation-efficient than pre-training from the ground up. Experimental findings indicate the resulting model displays strong zero-shot performance for multimodal generation, including tasks like image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. For instance, the model achieves a 44.5% accuracy in a zero-shot setting on the VQAv2 dataset, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art zero-shot model with a sevenfold reduction in parameters. Furthermore, the distillation process maintains the PLM's original capacity for textual language generation and understanding, making our model versatile for proficient use in both unimodal and multimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: A Feature Embedding Approach for Training Student Networks
abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks are constrained from use on mobile devices by their substantial storage and computational requirements. Knowledge distillation offers a solution by transferring information from a large, trained teacher network to a compact student network for optimization. Many existing teacher-student methods add a large number of auxiliary parameters because they depend on extra fully-connected layers to link the intermediate layers of the teacher and student. In this work, we propose a method to convey information from the teacher to the student that does not introduce new variables for optimization. Our approach re-envisions the teacher-student model through the lens of feature embedding. We introduce a locality preserving loss, which encourages the student network to produce low-dimensional features that retain the intrinsic properties of the corresponding high-dimensional features from the teacher. The compact network that results can therefore naturally achieve performance on par with the teacher network. We provide a theoretical analysis that confirms the lower computational complexity of our proposed method. Results from experiments on standard datasets and pre-trained networks indicate that our algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in both computational and storage efficiency.

author: White
title: Using Distillation to Create Portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are difficult to use on mobile devices for image-to-image translation because of their significant computation and storage demands. While network compression methods exist, they traditionally address visual recognition rather than generation tasks. Taking inspiration from knowledge distillation, we train a student generator having fewer parameters by transferring low-level and high-level information from a large, original teacher generator. To augment the student generator's capabilities, a student discriminator is also included to evaluate the distances between real images and those created by the student and teacher generators. This establishes an adversarial learning process for optimizing the student generator and student discriminator. Experiments performed on benchmark datasets, supported by qualitative and quantitative analysis, show that the proposed method can learn compact generative models that exhibit strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Specific BERT Compression Using Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: We introduce a method that automatically compresses BERT into task-adaptive smaller models for specific downstream tasks by utilizing differentiable Neural Architecture Search. This approach addresses the challenge of deploying large pre-trained language models like BERT, whose huge parameter sizes are a barrier for real-time applications with constrained resources. In contrast to existing methods that generate a single task-independent compressed model, our technique specializes the model for each task. The search is directed by a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss that provides hints, while an efficiency-aware loss acts as a constraint, enabling a strong balance between effectiveness and efficiency. When evaluated on several NLP tasks, the generated task-adaptive models demonstrate inference speeds 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT and are 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in parameter size, all while maintaining comparable performance.

author: Harrell
title: Inclusive Federated Learning Across Computationally Heterogeneous Devices
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a vital paradigm for privacy-preserving global model training on decentralized data. Many current FL methods presuppose that any participating client is capable of training the global model. In practice, however, client devices are often heterogeneous, possessing different levels of computing power. This presents a barrier to applying highly successful large models, such as BERT, in heterogeneous FL environments that include weak clients. Simplistic solutions, like omitting weaker clients or using a single small model for every client, create problems like under-representation of the excluded clients and lower accuracy due to data loss or insufficient model representational ability. We introduce a client-inclusive federated learning method to address this challenge. The core concept is to assign models of varying sizes to clients corresponding to their computational capacity, providing larger models to powerful clients and smaller models to weak ones. We also put forward an effective technique for sharing knowledge between multiple local models of different sizes. Consequently, every client can participate in model training under FL, and the final model can attain a large and powerful scale. Additionally, to better convey knowledge from the big models on powerful clients to small models on weak clients, we propose a momentum-based knowledge distillation method. The efficacy of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework is shown by extensive experiments on a variety of real-world benchmark datasets.

author: Evans
title: Creating Compact Metrics for Machine Translation through Learning
abstract: For machine translation and multilingual text generation, trained metrics like COMET or BLEURT have seen growing adoption. Treating evaluation as a regression problem, these metrics rely on representations from pre-trained multilingual models, for instance XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Studies on adjacent tasks suggest, however, that these models achieve peak efficiency at large sizes, which is impractical and costly for evaluation. We examine the trade-off between model capacity and multilinguality with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, on data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. Through a series of experiments, we first establish that model size is a considerable bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer. We then demonstrate a distillation-based solution to this bottleneck, which involves leveraging synthetic data and transferring knowledge from a single teacher model to several student models trained on related languages. Our approach provides an improvement of up to 10.5% over vanilla fine-tuning and attains 92.6% of the performance of RemBERT while using just a third of the parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Learning Visual Representations with Self-supervised Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This work addresses the application of self-supervised learning to small models. Our empirical findings indicate that widely used contrastive self-supervised learning techniques, while successful for training large models, do not perform well for smaller ones. As a solution to this issue, we present a new learning framework based on self-supervised distillation, which uses a larger teacher network to transfer its learned knowledge to a smaller student architecture. Rather than learning from unlabeled data directly, the student encoder is trained to emulate the similarity score distribution generated by the teacher across a sample of instances. We demonstrate that this method provides a dramatic performance increase for small networks on downstream tasks. On the ImageNet-1k dataset, our method improves the top-1 accuracy of EfficientNet-B0 from a self-supervised baseline of 42.2% to 67.6%, and for MobileNet-v3-Large, it raises the accuracy from 36.3% to 68.2%.

author: Lynch
title: Action Recognition through Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer from Vision to Sensors
abstract: The accuracy of human activity recognition (HAR) has recently been enhanced by multi-modal methodologies. However, the computational limitations of wearable devices like smartwatches prevent the direct application of these sophisticated methods. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes an end-to-end framework for distilling knowledge from the vision to the sensor modality. During the testing phase, this framework requires only time-series accelerometer data from the wearable hardware. The system therefore reduces the computational load on edge devices and also yields a learning model with performance closely approximating that of the computationally demanding multi-modal strategy. We transform the time-series data into two-dimensional images using a Gramian Angular Field (GAF) encoding technique to preserve local temporal relationships and accommodate visual deep learning models. In this work, we employed a ResNet18 as the teacher network and a multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as the student network. To reduce variations between the vision and sensor modalities, a novel loss function based on distance and angle-wise semantic knowledge is introduced. Comprehensive experimental evaluations on the UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets show the proposed model's effectiveness and competitiveness for deployment on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Efficient Novel View Synthesis via Knowledge Distillation from a Neural Radiance Field to a Neural Light Field
abstract: The high computational cost of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models presents a significant challenge for their practical application. Inference with NeRFs is slow because generating even a single pixel demands hundreds of queries to the network. While previous work has sought to address this by reducing the number of sampled points, the underlying requirement for iterative sampling remains. In contrast, the Neural Light Field (NeLF) provides a more direct representation for novel view synthesis, allowing a pixel to be rendered in a single forward pass without ray-marching. We introduce an approach that effectively learns the light field using a deep, 88-layer residual MLP network. We find that the crucial element for training such a deep NeLF is an adequate supply of training data. To provide this, we use data distillation to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world scenes confirm the superiority of our proposed method over competing algorithms. On synthetic datasets, we obtain a 26-35x reduction in FLOPs per camera ray and a 28-31x runtime acceleration, while also achieving substantially improved rendering quality (a 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR gain) compared to NeRF, all without needing any custom parallelism.

author: Farmer
title: Applying Knowledge Distillation to Develop Efficient Models for 3D Object Detection
abstract: High computational costs are a common problem for state-of-the-art 3D object detectors, despite significant advancements in the field. To address this, we investigate using knowledge distillation (KD) to create computationally efficient 3D detectors, concentrating on prevalent pillar- and voxel-based architectures. Given the scarcity of established teacher-student pairs, we first examine methods for producing student models with favorable balances of accuracy and speed, considering both model compression and reduced input resolution. We then present a benchmark based on six specifically constructed teacher-student pairs for assessing the application of existing 2D KD methods to 3D object detection. Furthermore, we put forward a new KD pipeline that contains an improved logit KD approach, which concentrates distillation on a small set of pivotal locations identified by the teacher's classification response. This pipeline also employs a teacher-guided initialization of the student model to promote the transfer of feature extraction capabilities via weight inheritance. We validate our methods with extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our highest-performing model obtains 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, exceeding its teacher while using only 44% of the teacher's flops. Our most efficient model operates at 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is 2.2 times faster than PointPillar and also achieves greater accuracy.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring Knowledge for Segmentation from a Multi-Modal Network to a Mono-Modal Network
abstract: Fusing information from multiple imaging modalities is known to improve medical image segmentation accuracy compared to single-modality methods. Despite this, clinical practice often limits data collection to a single modality due to constraints on cost, scan time, and the availability of scanners and physicians. We introduce a framework to distill knowledge from a trained multi-modal teacher network to a student network that operates on a single modality. This method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student model is trained with a single modality, a subset of the n modalities used by the teacher. We demonstrate the utility of our framework on the BraTS 2018 dataset for brain tumor segmentation. Using a variety of architectures, we find that the student network learns effectively from the teacher, leading to segmentation accuracy that is consistently superior to that of a baseline mono-modal network.

author: Osborne
title: Knowledge Distillation from Deep Neural Networks for Healthcare Applications
abstract: The rapid expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) creates significant opportunities and urgent requirements for Computational Phenotyping research to discover meaningful, data-driven patterns of disease. Deep Learning models deliver superior performance on robust prediction tasks in computational phenotyping, yet they are hampered by a lack of model interpretability, a crucial attribute for clinicians engaged in decision-making. We propose a novel knowledge-distillation method to acquire interpretable phenotype features that facilitate robust prediction while matching the performance of deep learning models. In our framework, Gradient Boosting Trees are used to learn interpretable features from deep learning models, including the Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Through exhaustive experiments with a real-world clinical time-series dataset, we show that our technique achieves performance that is similar or superior to that of the deep learning models and supplies interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

author: Moreno
title: A Learned Approach for Agile Quadrotor Flight in Obstacle-Dense Environments with Perception Constraints
abstract: For achieving minimum-time autonomous quadrotor navigation through obstacle-filled spaces, neural control policies have recently demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional model-based planning and control approaches. A significant limitation of these policies is their lack of perception awareness. This quality is essential for vision-based navigation, given the restricted field of view of a camera and the underactuated dynamics of the quadrotor. We introduce a system founded on learning principles to enable rapid, perception-aware flight within cluttered environments. Our technique unites imitation learning and reinforcement learning (RL) through a privileged learning structure. First, a perception-aware teacher policy with access to full-state information is trained with RL to traverse cluttered settings in minimal time. The knowledge from this policy is then distilled using imitation learning to a vision-based student policy, which must perceive its surroundings only with a camera. This approach, which tightly integrates perception and control, results in a major enhancement to the success rate and a tenfold increase in computation speed. We validate the closed-loop control performance via hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: An Adaptation and Distillation Method for Creating Small, Fast, and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Specific Domains
abstract: We introduce a general methodology for creating small, fast, and effective pre-trained models designed for specific domains. Our process involves adapting a generic, off-the-shelf pre-trained model and then performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation within the target domain. The adaptation phase includes a domain-specific vocabulary expansion, with the size of the incremental vocabulary determined automatically by corpus-level occurrence probability. Subsequently, we systematically investigate various strategies for compressing the large pre-trained model. This approach addresses the issues of domain shift, as well as fine-tuning and online deployment challenges related to latency and capacity, which are common when using large general models. Our experiments, conducted in the biomedical and computer science domains, show that the resulting models outperform BERT BASE on domain-specific tasks. The models are also 3.3 times smaller and 5.1 times faster than the BERT BASE model.

author: Nguyen
title: Applying Knowledge Distillation for the Creation of Compact Highway Networks
abstract: In recent years, deep learning has advanced the state-of-the-art for speech recognition. A challenge, however, is that neural network models are considerably larger than conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, which hinders their deployment on embedded devices. Our previous work explored compact highway deep neural networks (HDNNs), a class of depth-gated feedforward neural networks for acoustic modeling. We established that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve similar recognition accuracy to plain deep neural network (DNN) models but with a much smaller parameter count. This work extends these efforts by utilizing knowledge distillation, a technique also described as teacher-student training. Specifically, we employ a high-accuracy, cumbersome model to guide the training of a compact HDNN. We additionally investigate sequence training and adaptation within this teacher-student framework. Our experiments were carried out on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. Using this approach, we substantially improved the recognition accuracy of an HDNN acoustic model with fewer than 0.8 million parameters, and thereby closed the performance gap with a plain DNN containing 30 million parameters.
